Subscribe another address Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Link chatgptiseatingtheworld.com ↗ Posted by Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 On Tuesday, a U.S. federal appeals court ruled in favor of Thomson Reuters , upholding the company’s landmark win in a copyright infringement case against the now-defunct legal AI startup Ross Intelligence. The ruling marks the first federal appeals case to reject a fair use argument for using publisher content, without permission or compensation, to train a commercial AI product. “The undisputed evidence reflects that Thomson Reuters’s materials possess a creative spark, and ROSS aspired to be a direct competitor by using them for a highly similar purpose,” wrote Judge Tamika Montgomery-Reeves, who sits on the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia, in her decision . Notably, Montgomery-Reeves points out that the case does not concern a large-language model (LLM) or other generative AI tool. Ross’s competing AI search engine didn’t generate original text, but instead retrieved existing passages from judicial opinions. She argues that this may limit its impact on other AI copyright litigation. RELATED ARTICLE Trump administration says a New York Times win in OpenAI lawsuit would “threaten national security” and hurt small newsrooms Andrew Deck September 2, 2026 “Under ROSS’s framing, this case appears to concern the future of AI legal technology. But appearances can be deceiving,” she writes. “In truth, this is no more than an ordinary copyright case.” Thomson Reuters filed its lawsuit back in 2020, long before the release of ChatGPT and other generative AI chatbots as we know them. The first known AI copyright lawsuit in the U.S., the case echoes many more recent lawsuits between news publishers and AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. Thomson Reuters argued that Ross had copied thousands of “headnotes,” short summaries of the legal issues in a given case, that were published on its legal research platform Westlaw. These headnotes were then used to train Ross’s own competing AI-powered legal search engine. In a February 2025 ruling , judge Stephanos Bibas sided with Thomson Reuters in the case. He rejected the argument that using copyrighted work to train the commercial AI model was legally permissible, as Ross had argued in court. One of the main factors in a fair use case is whether the infringing work impacts the market value of the original. “Even taking all facts in favor of Ross, it meant to compete with Westlaw by developing a market substitute,” wrote Bibas in his original ruling. “And it does not matter whether Thomson Reuters has used the data to train its own legal search tools; the effect on a potential market for AI training data is enough.” Legal experts have been keeping a close eye on Ross’s appeal with the 3rd U.S Circuit Court of Appeal. As the first AI copyright case to reach a federal appeals court, there was potential for it to set far-reaching legal precedent on fair use — precedent that could be taken advantage of by news publishers arguing in similar AI copyright cases. RELATED ARTICLE What it takes to sue OpenAI as a journalism nonprofit Andrew Deck June 25, 2025 Ultimately, Montgomery-Reeves’ ruling emphasizes that an AI tool that reproduces a copyrighted work’s text in order to compete directly with that work in the market, will likely not hold up to a fair use test. But she leaves room for generative AI tools to be considered more transformative than Ross’s AI search engine. In the lawsuit Bartz vs. Anthropic, filed by members of the Authors Guild , a judge ruled that Anthropic’s use of published books to train its Claude LLMs was, in fact, fair use. It was only Anthropic’s decision to pirate books and store copies of them that lost them in that case. That ruling in June 2025 resulted in the largest settlement in U.S. copyright law history, granting a $1.5 billion payout to authors and publishers . “Unlike the AI models in Bartz …ROSS’s AI platform cannot generate original expression, and the evidence here supports the opposite conclusion about transformativeness,” wrote Montgomery-Reeves, implying that her ruling does not contradict the ruling in that case. In other words, if Ross had built a product that could output summaries of Westlaw’s headnotes with its own “original expression,” this fair use ruling could have looked very different. Subscribe another address Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions. Meta-owned platforms include Facebook, WhatsApp, Oculus, Threads, Instagram, and Messenger. (Adobe Stock) By Andrew Deck and Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 17, 2026, 2:30 p.m. RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models. In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts. On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then. “I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'” Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.” Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place. As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold): You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products . Here’s the original text : You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains , web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train , and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements . The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.” Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 ★ Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Adding this language to more general terms of service, and allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products,” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s scraping permissions. A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “ Ad Creative Generative AI Terms ” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand. Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements. “[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.” University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house. “You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said. RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 At least three journalism organizations have publicly raised concerns about the forthcoming terms as a result of Nieman Lab’s reporting. Prior to the update on Friday, the European Publishers Council announced that it would formally petition the E.U.’s telecommunications regulatory authorities and its executive body, the European Commission, to “ scrutinize these terms urgently, including their implications for copyright, contractual fairness and abuse of market power .” The United Kingdom News Media Association , the trade organization representing British media, issued a statement on Friday calling for government officials to intervene. “This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber . “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.” The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “ outrageous and probably illegal .” “The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power,” Coffey said. “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.” This story has been updated to include comments from Meta. results.pageDescription: Wrappers around the xml2 and httr packages to make it easy to download, then manipulate, HTML and XML.
results.evidenceText:
Easily Harvest (Scrape) Web Pages • rvest Skip to content rvest Overview rvest helps you scrape (or harvest) data from web pages. It is designed to work with magrittr to make it easy to express common web scraping tasks, inspired by libraries like beautiful soup and RoboBrowser . If you’re scraping multiple pages, I highly recommend using rvest in concert with polite . The polite package ensures that you’re respecting the robots.txt and not hammering the site with too many requests. Installation # The easiest way to get rvest is to install the whole tidyverse: install.packages ( "tidyverse" ) # Alternatively, install just rvest: install.packages ( "rvest" ) Usage library ( rvest ) # Start by reading a HTML page with read_html(): starwars <- read_html ( "https://rvest.tidyverse.org/articles/starwars.html" ) # Then find elements that match a css selector or XPath expression # using html_elements(). In this example, each
corresponds # to a different film films <- starwars |> html_elements ( "section" ) films #> {xml_nodeset (7)} #> [1]

The Phantom Menace

Released: 1999 ... #> [2]

Attack of the Clones

Released: 20 ... #> [3]

Revenge of the Sith

Released: 200 ... #> [4]

A New Hope

Released: 1977-05-25 ... #> [5]

The Empire Strikes Back

Released: ... #> [6]

Return of the Jedi

Released: 1983 ... #> [7]

The Force Awakens

Released: 2015- ... # Then use html_element() to extract one element per film. Here # we the title is given by the text inside

title <- films |> html_element ( "h2" ) |> html_text2 ( ) title #> [1] "The Phantom Menace" "Attack of the Clones" #> [3] "Revenge of the Sith" "A New Hope" #> [5] "The Empire Strikes Back" "Return of the Jedi" #> [7] "The Force Awakens" # Or use html_attr() to get data out of attributes. html_attr() always # returns a string so we convert it to an integer using a readr function episode <- films |> html_element ( "h2" ) |> html_attr ( "data-id" ) |> readr :: parse_integer ( ) episode #> [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 If the page contains tabular data you can convert it directly to a data frame with html_table() : html <- read_html ( "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Lego_Movie&oldid=998422565" ) html |> html_element ( ".tracklist" ) |> html_table ( ) #> # A tibble: 29 × 4 #> No. Title `Performer(s)` Length #> #> 1 1. results.pageDescription: The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company's new…
results.evidenceText: Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites | Nieman Journalism Lab Get Nieman Lab in your inbox. All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites. Leave this empty Email address Name (optional) Subscribe We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email? Nearly there — check your email. We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder. Subscribe another address (Photo by Dima Solomin on Unsplash ) Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites Link newsmediaalliance.org ↗ Posted by Hanaa' Tameez October 22, 2026 The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30. In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.” The terms, first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15 , would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is currently no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping. “News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey said in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their users), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.” NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey said, should focus on four core issues: (i) the specific Meta Company Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content; (ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products; (iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized; (iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected. Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.” The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its new subscription service, Meta One, which requires users to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world. The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute published its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.” “If Meta gets away with this, every dominant technology company will have a blueprint for doing the same,” said CMDG director Courtney Radsch . “Regulators have an opportunity to draw a line now, before the next generation of AI monopolies is built on the uncompensated work of journalists, publishers, and creators.” Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 ★ Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Meanwhile, publishers’ and media advocates’ concerns about the new terms of service are mounting in Europe. On Thursday morning, the Movement for an Open Web (MOW) — a U.K. nonprofit organization that advocates for an accessible internet — filed formal complaints with the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission’s Directorate General for Competition, calling the terms “unfair,” and “exploitative” and saying they “threaten to cause immediate and irreparable harm to businesses.” “The terms go live in a few days’ time, and once they’re in force the damage will be done — you can’t unscrape that content,” said Tim Cowen , a MOW cofounder. MOW’s complaints follow comments from CMA executive director for digital markets Will Hayter , who said during a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday that he had sent a letter to Meta and scheduled a meeting with company representatives to learn more about the terms. In Germany, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers also sent a joint letter to the European Commission, calling on the institution to block the new terms from going into effect until it conducted a complete review. On Wednesday, four European press associations — the European Magazine Media Association, the European Newspaper Publishers’ Association, the European Press Council, and News Media Europe — sent a joint letter to the European Commission and its heads of technology and competition. The letter, viewed by Nieman Lab, claims that Meta’s new terms violate the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region. The joint letter calls on the Commission to block the terms from “taking effect in their current wording — or in any wording producing identical or similar effects — to safeguard publishers’ rights.” “Publishers, whose content has long been subject to sweeping unfair and unlawful exploitation by dominant gatekeepers, including for AI-related purposes, thus face an unacceptable choice: abandon a key distribution channel or consent to the exploitation of their professional content without negotiation, licensing and remuneration,” the letter reads. “These conditions could also undermine publishers’ rights in ongoing or future AI-related legal proceedings.” RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 The Association of Information Media (AMI) in Spain, which represents more than 100 news outlets in the country, echoed its support of the letter in a statement on Thursday. “Technological innovation and the development of artificial intelligence cannot come at the expense of content creators’ rights or the economic viability of professional journalism,” the AMI statement reads in part. “ Defending publishers’ rights does not mean hindering innovation, but rather ensuring that it develops while respecting the law, competition, and media pluralism.” Read the full News/Media Alliance letter here . results.evidenceText: Spatial Reserves | A guide to public domain spatial data and societal issues Spatial Reserves A guide to public domain spatial data and societal issues Home Spatial Reserves About the book About the authors Exercises and data for the book Related sites SM Datum: A Free Browser Toolkit That Meets Spatial Data Where It Is 2026 16 Nov josephkerski Leave a comment As our book and this blog is focused on spatial data, this essay describing a rich and functional set of tools to work with spatial data should be of interest to many. With my thanks to Puneet from SM Datum for this post! “Much of the friction in working with spatial data happens before any analysis begins. A colleague sends a zipped shapefile, a field team returns a spreadsheet of GPS points, a student downloads Landsat scenes as a folder of separate band files, or a planning office shares a KMZ drawn in Google Earth. Each of these is perfectly good data, but each arrives in a different shape. Too often, the first hour of a project goes into converting, re-projecting and repairing files simply so that a tool will accept them. We built SM Datum ( https://smdatum.com ) to remove as much of that friction as possible, in a web browser, at no cost. SM Datum is a free, browser-based GIS toolkit with 16 tools and more than 70 operations, from format conversion and reprojection to vector analysis, terrain and hydrology, remote sensing and print-ready map layouts. What we hope will interest readers of this blog most is the range of data it accepts as it comes. On the vector side, that means Shapefiles (zipped, or simply the folder of .shp, .dbf, .shx and .prj files), GeoJSON, GeoPackage, KML and KMZ, and ordinary CSV, TSV and Excel files. Spreadsheets do not need to be tidied first: geometry can be built from latitude and longitude columns, a WKT column or a coordinate-sequence column, and common column names are detected automatically. On the raster side, it reads GeoTIFF, ERDAS IMAGINE, ASCII Grid, JPEG2000 and SRTM .hgt elevation files. Coordinates can even be typed or pasted in DMS, decimal degrees, UTM or MGRS. Satellite imagery is where we have tried hardest to help. Landsat and Sentinel-2 downloads usually arrive as separate single-band files, and Landsat’s older and newer sensors use different band numbers for the same colours, which quietly produces wrong NDVI maps when bands are mixed up. In SM Datum, the user picks the sensor (Landsat 4/5, 7, 8/9 or Sentinel-2) and receives correctly labelled upload slots, and the bands are stacked automatically. A pre-stacked file works too, and an area-of-interest boundary crops the scene before processing. From there, NDVI, NDWI and NDBI can be calculated, or the land cover classified automatically into water, vegetation, built-up and bare soil, refined with the user’s own samples, and exported with a PDF report of area by class. Two design choices shape the rest of the platform. First, users choose the result rather than the steps. Asking for a watershed from a DEM runs depression filling and flow direction automatically, and returns a watershed polygon with its area. Second, tools connect to each other, so the output of one can move straight into the next: for example, repair a file’s geometry, reproject it, buffer it and lay out a map, with a single download at the end. All geoprocessing runs on the server in projected units, so a 500-metre buffer is 500 metres wherever it is drawn. Because this blog rightly encourages readers to think critically about cloud tools, we want to be clear about how data is handled and where the limits are. Files are processed in memory for each request and discarded immediately afterwards; nothing is stored, and no account is required. There are no advertisements and no daily or monthly usage limits. SM Datum is free to use but is not open source, it needs an internet connection, and uploads are limited to 50 MB per file for most tools and up to 200 MB for imagery. Results such as land-cover classification are useful for teaching and rapid assessment, but they are not a substitute for ground-truthed, survey-grade work. Uploading Sentinel-2 or Landsat bands as downloaded. SM Datum labels the band slots for the chosen sensor and stacks them automatically. The above graphic shows a plain CSV of 16 lakes, dams and towns in Rajasthan, India, previewed in KML Studio before export. Latitude and longitude columns were detected automatically and the points grouped into three categories, ready to download as KML or KMZ for Google Earth.” I look forward to your comments. –Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data The NSDI Strategic Plan 2025-2035 2026 2 Nov josephkerski 6 comments As our book and this Spatial Reserves blog are focused on spatial data, we have discussed the National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI) as an important guiding document for spatial data production, management, and dissemination in the USA many times in this blog space. The NSDI, as defined in the Geospatial Data Act of 2018 (43 U.S.C. 46), is—“… the technology, policies, criteria, standards, and employees necessary to promote geospatial data sharing throughout the Federal Government, State, Tribal, and local governments, and the private sector (including nonprofit organizations and institutions of higher education).” I clearly remember the day I was working at USGS, way back in 1994, when Nancy Tosta of FGDC addressed my colleagues and I with the first bold vision of NSDI. I had a distinct impression that we were not simply creating DEMs and DLGs and DOQs, but were contributing to something much grander and far reaching. The Federal Geographic Data Committee (FGDC) has developed a new strategic plan, Building the Geospatial Future Together – the NSDI Strategic Plan, for 2025 – 2035 . As described on the FGDC pages, the plan was developed with inputs from several sources, “including FGDC agencies, the National Geospatial Advisory Committee, and geospatial partner organizations. The plan expanded the previously more Federally-focused strategic plan and developed a broader nationally scoped plan, designed to encourage active engagement and leadership from multiple sectors.” The pages state that “The new plan presents a bold vision for the future of the NSDI in the U.S., emphasizing collaboration, partnerships, innovation, and technological advancement to create a seamlessly interconnected national geospatial ecosystem that delivers actionable insights to address the complex challenges of our time.” What are your thoughts on this statement and on the rigor of the plan? I like the goals stated up front, “This NSDI strategic plan is guided by three overarching goals: Governance, Data and Technology, and People” – recognizing that creating data is never “just about the data and tools.” The document states that “The overarching vision for the NSDI is that, by 2035, the NSDI will be a seamlessly interconnected national geospatial ecosystem” and I truly hope this will be the case, reducing redundancy in data gathering agencies, providing multiple ways of integrating that data into GIS workflows, and providing rich metadata so decision makers can make the wisest decisions possible. Indeed, the document includes “build once and use many times” and the FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable), which I salute. The application areas mentioned include disaster response, smart cities, health care, supply chain, and others. The document states that “Upon the approval of this strategic plan, the FGDC will begin developing an implementation plan that will include metrics and timelines for the completion of the goals and objectives outlined herein.” I have not been able to find this plan yet, and welcome any reader to point me to it on FGDC.GOV or elsewhere. I look forward to your thoughts, –Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data Tags: AI , artificial-intelligence , news , politics , technology The increasing spatial accuracy in maps at work and in everyday life 2026 19 Oct josephkerski 4 comments The increasing spatial accuracy in GIS and remote sensing work, and even in everyday mapping tools that we use is a fascinating phenomenon. In just a few years, even the details available on ordinary fitness apps, such as on mine shown here, have rapidly advanced to the point of showing individual trees in certain communities (below). I conducted my own survey as I noticed these trees, and in most cases, the locations were accurate, and those symbolized on the map as larger symbols were indeed larger than those nearby, on the ground. Could the app be using a local tree data set from this community? In this community where I was walking, I also noticed that the alleyways were shown on the basemap in my fitness app; for example, at the location I was standing, at the blue dot, below. Was there an alley there? I conducted some field tests: Alley shown on the map to the west of where I was standing. … and sure, enough, there was indeed an alleyway there! The alley shown on the basemap in the above fitness app. Contrast the above high resolution base map with my post using the same fitness app, comparing 2012 and 2015, here in my “walking on water” essay: Walking on Water? Revisiting Reflections on Resolution and Scale | Spatial Reserves This 2012 and 2015 coarse base map seems ancient, but it was only from the last decade! 2012: 2015: Such developments make tools in use everyday more interesting and more suited to our needs (is the bus really only 1 minute and 20 seconds from here? Sure enough, 1 minute and 20 seconds later, here it is at my stop!). Yet with increasing spatial and attribute accuracy is accompanied by increasing potential for treading on one’s location privacy. Indeed, is any of our locations truly private these days? See my related recent posts: Here, about my colleague who tried to be “off camera” in the community: Location Privacy: The plethora of cameras in the community | Spatial Reserves And blurring of images in ground photographs: Location Privacy: Update on Blurring of Images in Ground Photographs | Spatial Reserves And while inside buildings: Location Privacy While Shopping at Physical Stores | Spatial Reserves What are your thoughts on this topic as we head into the latter part of the 2020s? And for the educators reading this blog, how do you teach about this issue? In which courses do you do so? — Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data A Chatbot for a GIS Hub’s Data Library 2026 5 Oct josephkerski Leave a comment Examining the capabilities of GIS libraries and the implications for future use of spatial data has long been a theme of this blog. Another recurring theme in this blog has been the developments and implications of AI tools on GIS. The Cobb County Georgia ArcGIS Hub site is a good example of both a wonderfully functional data library as well as offering an innovative use of AI in obtaining meaningful information. A GIS chatbot was developed by the GIS analysts for Cobb County Georgia, to handle both public and internal inquiries in real time. To overcome the fact that most Large Language Models (LLMs) don’t have expertise in specific domains, the Cobb County staff developed something called Retrieval-Augmented Generation, which obtains relevant, up-to-date information from their GIS dataset and provides it as context for the model, which improves response quality and reliability. Here is the data served to the public via the county’s GIS hub site: https://geo-cobbcountyga.hub.arcgis.com/pages/get-data For more information, see my Esri colleague Jim Baumann’s article about the site and its capabilities, and why and how they developed the Chatbot capabilities, here: Get to Know Cobb County’s GIS Chatbot | Spring 2026 | ArcUser According to the above article, analyst Chunguang Zhang, said, “The GIS chatbot answers frequent GIS-related questions and queries, which reduces the need for human interaction and support. This improves response times and ensures consistency in the response. It also allows staff to quickly retrieve zoning information, parcel verification, address validation, and GIS application data.” Thus, the Chatbot is to serve both the internal staff as well as the general public. I especially like this part: “In developing the GIS chatbot, Zhang compiled years of resident inquiries and staff responses from GIS-related emails for training purposes. To ensure the consistency of the chatbot’s response, he leveraged ChatGPT to generate three similar variations of each question while keeping exactly the same answer. This ensured uniform and accurate responses every time.” I say “bravo” to this clever work. As an educator, I also appreciate the array of educational items on the county’s GIS site, too, such as these geospatial tools for the classroom and this “What is GIS?” story map: Intro to Geography & GIS in Cobb County | Cobb County GIS Hub Site . I anticipate AI tools becoming embedded in many ArcGIS Hub sites and other spatial data libraries. It has the potential to narrow the results that a data user can find, and potentially hinder the creative habits that humans have developed in the data acquisition skills building. But, done right, it also has the potential to enhance what could be found on such sites, as well as reduce data searching time for the analyst, allowing more time for analysis and synthesis, and other tasks. What is your reaction to the above? –Joseph Kerski Categories: Public Domain Data A Fully Online Course based on GIS and Society is now freely available 2026 21 Sep josephkerski 2 comments Would you like to take a course based on the following 3 important and relevant themes? Where to find spatial data . How to critically evaluate that data . Societal issues surrounding data: Copyright, data quality, ethics, location privacy, AI, and others. A course focusing on the above 3 themes is now freely available via a self-paced online course, linked below. This course contains selected, pertinent content of our book and blog Spatial Reserves; and in addition, hands-on engaging exercises where you grapple with concepts of: Scale Uncertainty Ethics and other issues in a decision-making GIS environment. I have rigorously tested, taught, refined, and evaluated this course in higher education full-semester settings, short courses, online and face-to-face, in a wide variety of settings for a wide diversity of GIS data users and analysts in multiple locations around the world. The course is served as a story map collection, available here. Here is a playlist of the course videos: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLL_rej_JJ9qk&si=rIdPRLtIyLG04Pd9 It is also described in the following essay: https://community.esri.com/t5/education-blog/a-new-complete-course-in-data-gis-and-society/ba-p/1402213 Plus, the course is also served as an ArcGIS Experience, here: https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/726bab5044f74bb4a1de4965de679c7d This course invites learners to work with real data to solve problems and foster skills through a set of readings, hands-on activities, discussions, quizzes, and a final project.  I also invite instructors who seek to incorporate meaningful data and discussion about data in their courses to use all or part of this course in their own courses and programs. The Course is served as a story map collection and as an ArcGIS Experience (both shown above). Course Description:   Geospatial data are the foundation upon which GIS and spatial analysis rests. As GIS has matured, the challenge has evolved from generating data to managing the enormous volume of data from government agencies, nonprofit organizations, and industry, and increasingly, from ordinary citizens through citizen science and volunteered geographic information efforts. Key to working with this volume of data are essential issues such as privacy, copyright, public domain, cost recovery, metadata standards, and data quality that GIS professionals must grapple with to be effective in the 21st Century. This class discusses and applies these issues and works with a rich array of data sources to enable effective decision-making in a Geographic Information System.  The prerequisite for this course is an introductory GIS course or similar GIS course and/or work experience. Course Questions: The course is focused on three questions: 1.  How can I find geospatial data for my projects? 2.  How do I know if I can trust the geospatial data that I find?   In other words, how can I assess geospatial data quality?  3.  How can I consider societal issues surrounding geospatial data and tools, including copyright, location privacy, ethics, symbology, classification methods, map projections, and others?  Course Philosophy:  Four philosophies run through the course: 1.  Data is the foundation for all mapping, analysis, and decision-making that stems from that mapping and analysis.  Thus, data and data quality are vitally important to continually ask questions about, to seek, and to assess. 2.  Scale matters.  Patterns and relationships may exist at one scale and not another, and vice versa.  The scale at which you are conducting your analysis and the scale at which your data has been collected and published have great influences on the patterns that you will see, and the patterns that will remain hidden. 3.  You will encounter data that is understandable, and data that is confusing.    You will encounter data portals that are easy-to-use, and others that are difficult.  This is intentional:  The course instructor is not cleaning up any of the data or the data sites.  You will encounter the exact same thing in the workplace, and learning how to deal with geo-data challenges is central to the objectives of this course. 4.  Today’s GIS tools and open data portals are easier to use than ever before.  However, learning GIS is not just learning software interfaces and where data are located.  Central to successful use of GIS and to this course is cultivating a  healthy critical view of data and of GIS tools–recognizing their benefits, and also their limitations.   Course Themes: Weekly themes of this course include: Week 1:  Spatial data and the public domain.    GIS in our everyday lives.   Week 2:  Vector data model and data, portals, data quality.  Week 3:  Raster data model and data, portals, location privacy.  Week 4:  Data costs, local data access.  Week 5:  Metadata and standards.  National and state data portals.   Week 6:   National and international data infrastructures and initiatives.   Week 7:  Data policies.   Week 8:  Crowdsourced data.  Data disclaimers.  Week 9:  Cloud computing and GIS.  Software as a service.  Week 10:  The future of public domain spatial data.     Course Prerequisites and History: This 10 week online course was created for a graduate program inside a university GIS program.  This course is meant to follow an introductory course covering basic GIS skills.  I have taught, assessed, and improved this course each year over the span of over 20 years and am happy to share it with the community.  The course was originally taught face-to-face, then taught online via a Learning Management System (LMS), and then moved into a space so that you can access it, above.   Course Issues, Skills, Data Sets, and Portals: Major issues addressed include:   Data sources, data representation and models, data quality, metadata, spatial data input and output, spatial analysis, location privacy, copyright, streaming vs. downloading data, on premises servers vs. open access, spatial data serving policy.   Major skills addressed include:  spatial data management, analyzing tabular information, data input and querying, locating spatial data, assessing spatial data, formatting spatial data, projecting, georeferencing, geocoding, overlay and proximity, merging, raster data analysis, preparing 3D visualizations, making decisions with GIS and data. Subscribe another address Two out of five Americans regularly get their news on Facebook Link pewresearch.org ↗ Posted by Hanaa' Tameez October 20, 2026 Despite what my Facebook feed looks like, the platform’s not just for AI fruit videos and birthday posts. According to data from the Pew Research Center published Monday, 40% of adults in the United States regularly get their news from Facebook. That’s up from 36% in 2020, signaling the continued stability of the platform as a news source — a trend that the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism observed in its Digital News Report this year. As we reported in June, people around the world are increasingly abandoning news websites for social media. The Center surveyed 5,600 U.S. adults in late August as part of its American Trends Panel, and asked respondents several questions about their news and social media habits. Pew did not give respondents a definition of “news,” instead letting them use their own understanding of the term when they filled out the survey. More than half ( 59% ) said that they get news from social media “often or sometimes,” but only 19% actually prefer social media as a place to get news. Of Facebook news consumers, 33% are men and 49% are between the ages of 30 and 49. The platform is most popular for women (47%), Hispanic Americans (51%), Americans with a high school diploma or less (46%), and Republicans (43%). Regular news consumption among American users has increased on nine of the 12 social media platforms that Pew studied, including YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), Reddit, Nextdoor, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. News consumption has either dropped or stayed the same on Rumble, Truth Social, and Bluesky. The second-most regularly used platform among American adults is YouTube (34%), followed by Instagram (23%), TikTok (20%), and X (10%). YouTube news consumers are more likely to be male (41%), between ages 18 and 29 (39%), and identify as Black (47%) or Asian (53%). Republicans (35%) and Democrats (36%) are equal YouTube news consumers. The most regularly used platform for news among young adults is Instagram (43%), followed by Facebook (40%), TikTok and YouTube (both 39%), and X and Reddit (both 18%). The Center found that 20% of U.S. adults now regularly get their news on TikTok, up from 3% in 2020. Of TikTok users, 53% reported getting news regularly on the platform. Nextdoor users are also increasingly turning to the neighborhood forum app for information. In 2026, 45% of Nextdoor users reported regularly getting news from the app, up from 23% in 2022. results.evidenceText: Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team - HOT Website HOT is a global community of mappers transforming lives using the power of open map data. Working in 94 countries, we collaborate with local communities, governments, and organizations to create and maintain detailed, accessible maps that aid local communities, NGOs, and governments in making informed decisions and improving lives. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(0) + 1}`" > Conflict & Displacement Our goal is to use open maps and data to strengthen humanitarian efforts in complex emergencies, helping to deliver life-saving aid and support projects for vulnerable communities. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(1) + 1}`" > Learn and Connect Empowering a global network of mappers and community leaders with the skills, knowledge, and connections to drive local humanitarian impact and build long-term resilience 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(2) + 1}`" > Disaster Response Disaster response has been at the heart of HOT's mission since its inception. Originating with the Haiti earthquake in 2010, HOT’s responses to major disasters have marked critical milestones in the organization’s history. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(3) + 1}`" > Disaster Risk Reduction Strengthening communities, governments, and partners with open geospatial data and tools to improve disaster mitigation, preparedness, and recovery for informed local decision-making and long-term resilience. 2, }" :style="`order: ${fixedIndex(4) + 1}`" > Urban Development Advancing locally-led open mapping and inclusive urban data production to bring vulnerable and underserved communities into view and strengthen evidence-based urban planning in rapidly growing cities. Impact Areas HOT works to solve local challenges that are global in scale and contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). We work in five core impact areas, and by driving efforts in these key areas work towards our mission to improve well-being, reduce suffering, and increase resilience for people who are systematically underrepresented in countries at high risk of disaster, humanitarian emergency and multidimensional poverty, through making and using open map data. 1 && getRelCar(0) 3 && getRelCar(0) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(0) + 1}`" > Disaster Response 1 && getRelCar(1) 3 && getRelCar(1) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(1) + 1}`" > Climate Resilience & Sustainability 1 && getRelCar(2) 3 && getRelCar(2) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(2) + 1}`" > Public Health 1 && getRelCar(3) 3 && getRelCar(3) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(3) + 1}`" > Displacement & Safe Migration 1 && getRelCar(4) 3 && getRelCar(4) 4, }" :style="`order: ${getRelCar(4) + 1}`" > Gender Equality Disaster Response The rising impact and scale of humanitarian emergencies on vulnerable populations make the demand for data-driven disaster response even more pressing. Open geospatial data provides government agencies and first responders with critical information to take more informed and locally appropriate action when a disaster or humanitarian crisis hits. Learn More Climate Resilience & Sustainability Open mapping supports strategies to mitigate potential climate impacts, enhance community preparedness, and ensure that communities grow in environmentally sustainable ways. Through mapping climate hazards and realities in the communities, local players can contribute towards finding sustainable solutions by filling in data gaps and contributing to long-term community resilience and development. Learn More Public Health When communities actively participate in mapping their own areas, they create detailed maps that help identify gaps and plan targeted and effective health interventions, ultimately improving the health and well-being of communities globally. Thus, open geospatial data is invaluable for developing policies that address health disparities, enhance equitable health access, and evaluate the effectiveness of public health programs. Learn More Displacement & Safe Migration Conflict, persecution, violence, and natural disasters have caused a record more than 100 million people worldwide to be displaced . Humanitarian organizations and governments require accurate geospatial data to locate and understand the needs of displaced communities, identify potential risks, enable better coordination and resource allocation, and ensure that assistance reaches those who need it most. Learn More Gender Equality By identifying and addressing gender-specific gaps, open geospatial data provides a more nuanced understanding of how resources, services, and vulnerabilities are distributed across different genders within communities, ensuring an inclusive approach and community ownership in the open mapping process. HOT is committed to fostering inclusivity, and by involving women and gender non-conforming people in mapping initiatives, we ensure their needs are prioritized, enabling targeted and effective interventions to promote gender equity and inclusion. Learn More HOT works around the globe to support the use of OpenStreetMap by local communities and help build a local open mapping movement. HOT works across sectors to provide map data that revolutionizes disaster management, reduces risks, and contributes to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Who We Are Open Mapping Hubs HOT works through four regional Hubs to support and scale OpenStreetMap communities around the world. Regional Hubs leverage local expertise and resources to create and sustain the open mapping movement. Hubs have a pivotal role in facilitating localized mapping efforts and serve as a vital connection between local communities, NGOs, governments, and international aid organizations, ensuring that mapping initiatives are tailored to regional needs and priorities. Learn More Ready to get started creating and using open data? At HOT, we use a combination of open mapping tools developed by the open-source community to create, access, manage, analyze, and share open map data that serves our partners and local communities. All of these tools and resources are freely available for you to use. Tools & Resources Anyone can get involved in open mapping with HOT! Open mapping helps solve many problems around the world, and the mapping community welcomes you. Join us in making a difference! Your support helps us create impactful change in our community. Palesa joined an intensive residency at the African Drone and Data Academy, based at the Malawi University of Science and Technology. She started with zero flight hours. She finished with three remote pilot certifications after using drone mapping, GIS, and AI to tackle public health challenges. Her training is part of Design Thinking for Drone and Data Technology for the Youth Force. The initiative is building a new generation of certified youth drone mappers. It brings together the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT), UNICEF, the African Drone and Data Academy, Generation Unlimited, the Lesotho Aviation Authority, and Yoma. Subscribe another address Sinclair’s new Substack repackages its local TV reporting into a video podcast Link axios.com ↗ Posted by Hanaa' Tameez October 7, 2026 “How young is too young for a life in prison?” “SpaceX debris is washing ashore. Who’s responsible?” “Why schools get paid even when students fail.” Those are the top headlines so far on Sinclair Broadcasting Group’s new Substack publication, The National Press , launched this week. The National Press repackages some of the top stories from Sinclair’s 178 local news stations — which employ around 1,200 journalists — into a daily, 30-minute broadcast-style show. The program is hosted by former Newsmax and Christian Cable Network anchor Lyndsay Keith , who summarizes the stories and interviews the local journalists who first reported them. In the videos, Keith sits at a desk with a microphone; the dimly lit background is illuminated just enough to make out two American flags in a mug. (It gives off a true-crime YouTube podcast vibe.) As Axios’s Sara Fischer noted on Tuesday , Sinclair has long been accused of conservative bias in its local news operation. The National Press is launching in partnership with New Media, the company behind Bari Weiss’s The Free Press, and the two publications look somewhat alike (in part because they both run on Substack). New Media staffers will help create the content and maintain the site and the company will take a portion of Sinclair’s revenue from Substack, Fischer reported. The National Press is currently free to access, but has paid tiers that include ad-free viewing, community chat access, and merch. Subscriptions start at $5 per month or $50 per year. The five posts on the site so far have between seven and 14 likes each. Wednesday’s episode focuses on a story about how Michigan is reconsidering lifetime sentences for people sentenced between the ages of 18 and 20. It also tackles AI regulation debates in Congress, drawing on reporting by Capitol Hill reporter Ahtra Elnashar. The show doesn’t appear to be filmed in one take like a true TV news broadcast (Keith is first seen in a black blazer, then a brown one, before switching back to black by the end of the video). Another video, “ Worth Noticing: School Bus Incidents ,” is just two minutes long and compiles stories of school bus crashes from around the country. From the text accompanying the video: We trust school buses to get our kids from the safety of our homes to school every day. So why are we seeing so many serious injuries and incidents? Is this simply a string of unrelated tragedies? Are staffing shortages the problem here? Training gaps? Weak safety protocols? We’re going to be following these stories. Have you seen incidents like this in your community? Is this something that is keeping you awake at night? Because these stories are horrific; we’re talking about every parent’s nightmare. The National Press isn’t Sinclair’s first effort to reach a younger, video-first audience. In 2015, it launched millennial-focused news site Circa , which shuttered four years later. U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline Link parliamentlive.tv ↗ Posted by Andrew Deck , Hanaa' Tameez October 21, 2026 The U.K. competition and consumer protection authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss its new commercial terms of service. On Tuesday, Will Hayter , the executive director for digital markets at the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), shared the update during a session of the communications and digital committee of British Parliament , after a member of the House of Lords pressed him about Meta’s new terms. Hayter said he scheduled a meeting with the tech giant today to seek clarity on the new terms, though the CMA declined to provide any further details. RELATED ARTICLE Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes Andrew Deck October 17, 2026 Last week, Nieman Lab broke the news that the terms would permit mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. The new terms are slated to take effect on October 30, and there is currently no option to opt out. Virtually every news organization owns at least one Meta business account. “Are you going to pause the deadline? I mean, [it’s in] a week,” Veronica Wadley, Baroness Fleet and a former editor of the Evening Standard, said during the session of Parliament. “You know this includes almost every U.K. news publisher and it is clearly uncompetitive leverage of Meta’s strategic market position.” In the same session, Sarah Cardell , the CEO of CMA, said the authority had limited intervention options because it has not formally designated Meta as an “entrenched market power” (something it has done in the past for Google and Apple ). Cardell said other competition enforcement actions are a possibility, but the CMA is “urgently” seeking more information from Meta before making any judgment. Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 ★ U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Over the weekend, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping. A Meta spokesperson said on Saturday that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. “Does Meta think we can’t read?” Theo Bamber , chief executive of the U.K.’s News Media Association, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Monday. “We know you’ve taken the word ‘train’ out but changing it to ‘develop’ isn’t fooling anyone.” News publisher associations across Europe have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect next week. On Tuesday, two major German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review had been conducted. Together, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers represent more than 9,000 media brands across Europe. RELATED ARTICLE Meet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAI Andrew Deck February 20, 2025 “Meta intends to automatically capture, copy, and store the complete websites and archives of publishers and analyze them for its own automated and non-automated commercial products,” reads a joint statement from the associations . “This makes access to Meta’s platforms contingent on the free surrender of the entire digital publishing product. This is blatant theft.” The statement alleges that Meta’s new terms could be in violation of the E.U. Digital Markets Act, which was passed in 2022 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region. The publishers cited a specific clause that guarantees “fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory general conditions of access for business users.” The uproar from European publishers echoes similar opposition to the new terms from major U.S. publisher associations. Jason Kint, the CEO of Digital Content Next, has been vocal about his skepticism of the new terms since Nieman Lab’s story broke last week. “Meta’s supposed Friday night correction to its new commercial terms is a farce,” he wrote in a statement published on Tuesday. “Exactly what you’d expect from a gatekeeper notorious for abusing its market power.” Get Nieman Lab’s Daily Digest The most important stories about journalism and the future of news, delivered to your inbox every afternoon. results.title: GeoPandas
results.evidenceText: GeoPandas 1.2.1.dev0.dev+g199fc53c8 — GeoPandas 1.2.1.dev0+g199fc53c8.d20260928 documentation Skip to main content Back to top Ctrl + K System Settings Light Dark GitHub GeoPandas 1.2.1.dev0.dev+g199fc53c8 # GeoPandas is an open source project to make working with geospatial data in python easier. GeoPandas extends the datatypes used by pandas to allow spatial operations on geometric types. Geometric operations are performed by shapely . Geopandas further depends on pyogrio for file access and matplotlib for plotting. Description # The goal of GeoPandas is to make working with geospatial data in python easier. It combines the capabilities of pandas and shapely, providing geospatial operations in pandas and a high-level interface to multiple geometries to shapely. GeoPandas enables you to easily do operations in python that would otherwise require a spatial database such as PostGIS. Getting started Documentation About GeoPandas Community Useful links # Binary Installers (PyPI) | Source Repository (GitHub) | Issues & Ideas | Q&A Support Supported by # The GeoPandas project uses an open governance model and is fiscally sponsored by NumFOCUS . Consider making a tax-deductible donation to help the project pay for developer time, professional services, travel, workshops, and a variety of other needs.

results.pageTitle: spaCy · Industrial-strength Natural Language Processing in Python
results.pageDescription: spaCy is a free open-source library for Natural Language Processing in Python. It features NER, POS tagging, dependency parsing, word vectors and more.
results.evidenceText: spaCy · Industrial-strength Natural Language Processing in Python Get things done spaCy is designed to help you do real work — to build real products, or gather real insights. The library respects your time, and tries to avoid wasting it. It's easy to install, and its API is simple and productive. Blazing fast spaCy excels at large-scale information extraction tasks. It's written from the ground up in carefully memory-managed Cython. If your application needs to process entire web dumps, spaCy is the library you want to be using. Awesome ecosystem Since its release in 2015, spaCy has become an industry standard with a huge ecosystem. Choose from a variety of plugins, integrate with your machine learning stack and build custom components and workflows. Edit the code & try spaCy spaCy v 3.7 · Python 3 · via Binder run Features Support for 75 + languages 84 trained pipelines for 25 languages Multi-task learning with pretrained transformers like BERT Pretrained word vectors State-of-the-art speed Production-ready training system Linguistically-motivated tokenization Components for named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, sentence segmentation, text classification , lemmatization, morphological analysis, entity linking and more Easily extensible with custom components and attributes Support for custom models in PyTorch , TensorFlow and other frameworks Built in visualizers for syntax and NER Easy model packaging , deployment and workflow management Robust, rigorously evaluated accuracy NEW Large Language Models: Integrating LLMs into structured NLP pipelines The spacy-llm package integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) into spaCy, featuring a modular system for fast prototyping and prompting , and turning unstructured responses into robust outputs for various NLP tasks, no training data required. Learn more From the makers of spaCy Prodigy: Radically efficient machine teaching Prodigy is an annotation tool so efficient that data scientists can do the annotation themselves, enabling a new level of rapid iteration. Whether you're working on entity recognition, intent detection or image classification, Prodigy can help you train and evaluate your models faster. Try it out Reproducible training for custom pipelines spaCy v3.0 introduces a comprehensive and extensible system for configuring your training runs . Your configuration file will describe every detail of your training run, with no hidden defaults, making it easy to rerun your experiments and track changes. You can use the quickstart widget or the init config command to get started, or clone a project template for an end-to-end workflow. To use it with 'spacy train' # you can run spacy init fill-config to auto-fill all default settings: # python -m spacy init fill-config ./base_config.cfg ./config.cfg [ paths ] train = null dev = null vectors = null [ system ] gpu_allocator = null [ nlp ] lang = " en " pipeline = [] batch_size = 1000 [ components ] [ corpora ] [ corpora.train ] @readers = " spacy.Corpus.v1 " path = ${paths.train} max_length = 0 [ corpora.dev ] @readers = " spacy.Corpus.v1 " path = ${paths.dev} max_length = 0 [ training ] dev_corpus = " corpora.dev " train_corpus = " corpora.train " [ training.optimizer ] @optimizers = " Adam.v1 " [ training.batcher ] @batchers = " spacy.batch_by_words.v1 " discard_oversize = false tolerance = 0.2 [ training.batcher.size ] @schedules = " compounding.v1 " start = 100 stop = 1000 compound = 1.001 [ initialize ] vectors = ${paths.vectors} 🪐 Get started : pipelines/tagger_parser_ud The easiest way to get started is to clone a project template and run it – for example, this template for training a part-of-speech tagger and dependency parser on a Universal Dependencies treebank. $ python -m spacy project clone pipelines/tagger_parser_ud End-to-end workflows from prototype to production spaCy's new project system gives you a smooth path from prototype to production. It lets you keep track of all those data transformation , preprocessing and training steps , so you can make sure your project is always ready to hand over for automation. It features source asset download, command execution, checksum verification, and caching with a variety of backends and integrations. Try it out Get a custom spaCy pipeline, tailor-made for your NLP problem by spaCy's core developers. Streamlined. Nobody knows spaCy better than we do. Send us your pipeline requirements and we'll be ready to start producing your solution in no time at all. Production ready. spaCy pipelines are robust and easy to deploy. You'll get a complete spaCy project folder which is ready to spacy project run . Predictable. You'll know exactly what you're going to get and what it's going to cost. We quote fees up-front, let you try before you buy, and don't charge for over-runs at our end — all the risk is on us. Maintainable. spaCy is an industry standard, and we'll deliver your pipeline with full code, data, tests and documentation, so your team can retrain, update and extend the solution as your requirements change. Learn more In this free and interactive online course you’ll learn how to use spaCy to build advanced natural language understanding systems, using both rule-based and machine learning approaches. It includes 55 exercises featuring videos, slide decks, multiple-choice questions and interactive coding practice in the browser. Start the course Benchmarks spaCy v3.0 introduces transformer-based pipelines that bring spaCy's accuracy right up to the current state-of-the-art . You can also use a CPU-optimized pipeline, which is less accurate but much cheaper to run. results.evidenceText: Welcome to the QGIS Python API documentation project Welcome to the QGIS Python API documentation project Welcome to the QGIS Python API documentation project ¶ Introduction ¶ QGIS is a user friendly Open Source Geographic Information System (GIS) that runs on Linux, Unix, macOS, and Windows. QGIS supports vector, raster, and database formats. QGIS is licensed under the GNU General Public License. QGIS lets you browse and create map data on your computer. It supports many common spatial data formats (e.g. ESRI ShapeFile, GeoPackage, PostGIS, geotiff). QGIS supports plugins to do things like display tracks from your GPS. QGIS is Open Source software and it is free of cost ( download here ). We welcome contributions from our user community in the form of code contributions, bug fixes, bug reports, contributed documentation, advocacy and supporting other users on our mailing lists and forums. Financial contributions are also welcome. QGIS source code is available at https://github.com/qgis/QGIS . There is also a C++ version of the API documentation available. Versions of the API ¶ Documentation for master: https://qgis.org/pyqgis/master Documentation for current stable 4.4: https://qgis.org/pyqgis/4.4 Documentation for current LTR 3.44: https://qgis.org/pyqgis/3.44 See Backwards Incompatible Changes for information about incompatible changes to API between releases. Earlier versions of the documentation are also available as downloads: 4.2 , 4.0 , 3.42 , 3.40 , 3.38 , 3.36 , 3.34 , 3.32 , 3.30 , 3.28 , 3.26 , 3.24 , 3.22 , 3.20 , 3.18 , 3.16 , 3.14 , 3.12 , 3.10 , 3.8 , 3.6 , 3.4 , 3.2 , 3.0 . Communication channels ¶ For support we encourage you to join our mailing lists for users and developers. Some QGIS users and developers can also often be found in channels such as Matrix, Telegram,… Bug Reporting ¶ If you think you have found a bug in the documentation, please report it using our bug tracker . When reporting bugs, please be available to follow up on your initial report. results.evidenceText: Hacks/Hackers | Technology + Journalism Advancing media innovation & fostering public trust Since 2009, Hacks/Hackers has brought journalists and technologists together to build the future of news. See our programs → We do this by: 1/ Convening summits, forums and hackathons where journalists and technologists learn from each other and shape what comes next. 2/ Working directly with newsrooms through our Newsroom AI Lab, from scoping what you need to building it together. 3/ Sharing what we learn in the open through our newsletter, our own experiments with new tools and playbooks anyone can use. Upcoming events See all events on Luma Latest articles A $35,000 grant from the Reynolds Journalism Institute funds News Connectors, a pilot that opens to the public in early 2027.

results.pageDescription: From Data to Viz leads you to the most appropriate graph for your data. It links to the code to build it and lists common caveats you should avoid.
results.evidenceText: From data to Viz | Find the graphic you need What kind of data do you have? Pick the main type using the buttons below. Then let the decision tree guide you toward your graphic possibilities. Alternatively, check the complete decision tree . Numeric Categoric Num & Cat Maps Time series Network Swipe sideways to see the whole tree → Data Story From Data to Viz provides a decision tree based on input data format. This tree leads to twenty formats representing the most common dataset types. For each, an example of analysis based on real-life data is provided using the R programming language . Numeric Rbnb night prices on the french riviera Price / area relationship of 1500 apartments Evolution of the bitcoin price Relationship between life expectancy, gdp per capita and population Evolution of baby names in the US since 1880 Features of 32 famous car models Categoric Who sells more weapons? Caveats The best way to visualize data efficiently is probably to avoid the most common mistakes. From Data to Viz offers you a gallery of common caveats . Order your data When displaying the value of several entities, ordering it makes it way more insightful. To cut or not to cut? Cutting the Y axis is one of the most controversial practices in data viz. See why. The spaghetti chart A line graph with too many lines becomes unreadable: it is called a spaghetti graph. Pie chart The human eye is bad at reading angles. See how to replace the most criticized chart ever. Play with histogram bin size Always try different bin sizes when you build an histogram, it can lead to different insights. Do boxplots hide information? A boxplot is a great way to summarize a distribution but it hides the sample size and data distribution. The problem with error bars Barplots with error bars must be used with great care. Learn why and how to replace them. Too many distributions If you need to compare the distribution of many variables, don't clutter your graph. The rainbow color palette Avoid the rainbow color palette when you map a numeric variable. So many better palettes exist. Faceting: horizontal or vertical? More than 260 participants came together for four days of presentations, keynote lectures, workshops, poster sessions, discussions, and networking. Under the motto “Let’s transform cartography together” , EuroCarto 2026 provided a platform for researchers, professionals, and students to exchange ideas, share new developments, and discuss the future of cartography, geovisualization, and spatial technologies. The conference began on Tuesday, September 8, with pre-conference workshops , followed by the Opening Ceremony and Welcome Reception in the evening. Organized by the Czech Cartographic Society under the patronage of the International Cartographic Association , EuroCarto 2026 welcomed participants from across Europe and beyond, bringing together a diverse community with a shared interest in the transformation and future of cartography. Subscribe another address A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results Link idjc.syracuse.edu ↗ Posted by Sarah Scire October 15, 2026 Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received? It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could. In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories. The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.) The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr , director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough. “Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.” “The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.” RELATED ARTICLE Searching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalism Angie Drobnic Holan April 27, 2023 At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject. When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence. In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio ) more often than reporter-named accounts. The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here .
