results.title: ArchieML
results.pageDescription: ArchieML is a text format optimized for human writability. It was designed for users unfamiliar with existing serialization formats, and defines a forgiving, incremental parser that does not throw syntax errors.
results.evidenceText: Archie Markup Language (ArchieML) ArchieML ArchieML is a structured text format optimized for human writability. Resources Demo Usage Sandbox Spec Structured text, for an unstructured world. What is Archie Markup Language? ArchieML (or "AML") was created at The New York Times to make it easier to write and edit structured text on deadline that could be rendered in web pages, or more specifically, rendered in interactive graphics. One of the main goals was to make it easy to tag text as data, without having type a lot of special characters. Another goal was to allow the document to contain lots of notes and draft text that would not be read into the data. And finally, because we make extensive use of Google Documents's concurrent-editing features — while working on a graphic, we can have several reporters, editors and developers all pouring information into a single document — we wanted to have a format that could survive being edited by users who may never have seen ArchieML or any other markup language at all before. Why not YAML? Or JSON? ArchieML differs from other popular formats like YAML and JSON in several areas that we've found are key to making it easy to use: Whitespace is not significant to the document structure In YAML, lines must be indented precisely and variably; the wrong number of spaces to the left of a key invalidates the document, and tabs can't be used. AML ignores all whitespace not within a value. We believe this makes it easier for non-programmers to use, and is essential for use in environments with non-monospaced fonts, like in Google Documents. Unstructured text is ignored; there is no such thing as a parsing error AML was designed so that writers could work in a freeform environment. They should be able to add entire paragraphs as scratch work that do not appear in the output. JSON and YAML have strict schemas that forbid text deviating from a pattern. AML doesn't assume text follows any pattern. If it finds text that looks like data, it treats it as data. Otherwise, it moves on. The notation makes sense to non-programmers Lists of values are noted with bullet points / asterisks, not hyphens or quoted strings that must be separated with commas. An overriding goal was to have a intuitive format that could be passed to a non-technical user — a reporter, an assigning editor or a copy editor — to edit, and to have the format be clear enough that they could make changes without breaking the parsing of the document. If we were using another format, we'd have to explain indentation rules in YAML, or how to match curly braces or properly escape quotation marks in JSON, and so forth. How Does It Work in Practice? For a very simple example, here's a screenshot of the Google Doc that powers a recent graphic about the trick plays used by the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks: To generate the graphic, we load the ArchieML data from the document using the archieml-js npm module , then pass it to an underscore template to render the final markup server-side. This lets the journalists who are focusing on the text and content concentrate on getting the copy in shape independently of the developers working on the graphic. While this is a very simple example, with only a few bits of text and data and one comment at the end that is ignored, when we're covering a breaking news story, we can have a half-dozen people all contributing to a Google Doc at the same time as we gather all the information we need for a graphic and turn it into the final copy blocks that make their way into the finished piece. Resources Parsers and tools in (hopefully) your language of choice. JavaScript Both parsers can be used client-side in the browser, or using Asynchronous Module Definitions (AMD) such as RequireJS, and have test coverage. archieml-js Node Package Manager (npm) archieml-peg (by Jakub Dundalek ) archieml-loader is a Webpack loader for ArchieML files. grunt-archieml (by Andrew Chavez ) gulp-archieml (by Andrew Chavez / The Dallas Morning News) Ruby archieml-ruby is a Ruby parser for ArchieML. It is available through the RubyGems package manager, and has test coverage. RubyGems stream-cms is an elasticsearch backed archieml-to-json manager (by Jacqui Maher / BBC News Labs) R rchie (by Noam Ross ) .NET/C# archieml-net (by Roger Braunstein / Partlyhuman) PHP php-archieml (by Mathieu Gagnon ) Python archieml-python (by Brian Kim ) pip archieml-python (by Kevin Schaul ) Scala SArchieML (by Maciej Biłas ) HTML archieml-element is a Polymer 1.0 component for parsing ArchieML content (by Jay Pilgreen ) Clojure archieclj (by Michael Bauer ) Clojars Google Docs Plugins tools for connecting to Google Drive and parsing documents as ArchieML aml-gdoc-server (by David Yanofsky / Quartz) Node Package Manager (npm) grunt-google-archieml (by Ashlyn Still / The Atlanta Journal-Constitution) Node Package Manager (npm) Fusion Interactive Template (by Kit Cross / Fusion) node-archieml-boilerplate (by Stuart Thompson / The Wall Street Journal) googledoc-to-json (by Brad Oyler ) Node Package Manager (npm) Integrating with Google Documents At The New York Times, we normally write ArchieML in Google Documents. Both parsers include quick-start examples for how to download text from Google Docs and run it through the parser. They also include some formatting steps we take, such as converting links to HTML tags. Examples: JavaScript example Ruby example For more fully-fledged integrations with Google Docs, use one of the plugins above . Introductory Demo Click on any ArchieML textarea to try it out yourself, and see how changes affect the output. Or try out ArchieML in the Sandbox . Keys and values Strings can be stored as part of key/value pairs, defined whenever a line in ArchieML begins with a token followed by a colon. Keys can contain any unicode character, with the exception of whitespace / invisible characters, and a handful of characters that are used within ArchieML ( { } [ ] : . + ). The rest of the string is the value. key: This is a value ☃: Unicode Snowman for you and you and you! Whitespace surrounding keys and values is ignored. Indent as you like. Keys are case sensitive. 1: value 2:value 3 : value 4: value 5: value a: lowercase a A: uppercase A Lines that don't look like keys or other special commands are ignored: This is a key: key: value It's a nice key! Nested key structure Use dot-notation to create nested objects. colors.red: #f00 colors.green: #0f0 colors.blue: #00f You can also use "object" blocks to namespace a group of keys. {colors} red: #f00 green: #0f0 blue: #00f {} {numbers} one: 1 ten: 10 one-hundred: 100 {} key: value Dot notation can be used in object blocks as well: {colors.reds} crimson: #dc143c darkred: #8b0000 {} {colors.blues} cornflowerblue: #6495ed darkblue: #00008b {} You can close an object by beginning a line with {} . ArchieML is parsed one line at a time, so you can also close an object by opening a new one. {colors} red: #f00 green: #0f0 blue: #00f {numbers} one: 1 ten: 10 one-hundred: 100 {} key: value Nested object blocks Object blocks with names prepened with a period nest inside of open objects instead of ending them. Beginning a line with {} closes a nested object and returns to the parent. {colors} red: #f00 green: #0f0 blue: #00f {.numbers} one: 1 ten: 10 one-hundred: 100 {} nestedKey: nestedValue {months} january: 0 february: 1 Arrays of objects Groups of keys can be placed inside an array by giving the array a name within brackets. The name of the array can be any valid key, and can use dot-notation. You can optionally end an array with an empty set of brackets, or by beginning a new array. [scope.array] [] All keys inside the array are inserted into a single object within the array. The parser remembers the first key it found, and whenever it encounters it again, a new object is started. [arrayName] Jeremy spoke with her on Friday, follow-up scheduled for next week name: Amanda age: 26 # Contact: 434-555-1234 name: Tessa age: 30 [] Arrays of strings You can also create "simple" or "flat" arrays of strings. If an asterisk is encountered first within an array, that array will become a simple array, and key/value pairs within it will be ignored. If a key/value pairs is encountered first, then asterisk lines will be ignored. [days] * Sunday note: holiday! * Monday * Tuesday Whitespace is still fine around the '*' * Wednesday * Thursday Friday! * Friday * Saturday [] Nested arrays Array elements can contain arrays of their own. To begin an array while inside an array element, prepend its name with a period. [array] [.subarray] [.subsubarray] key: value Much like nested object blocks, nested arrays must be "closed" with empty brackets in order to move up to the parent level. [days] name: Monday [.tasks] * Clean dishes * Pick up room [] name: Tuesday [.tasks] * Buy milk [] Freeform arrays Freeforms are a third type of array that was created to have better control over presentation from within ArchieML. Unlike regular arrays, which group lines into objects whose values have no order, freeforms preserve the order of each of its lines . Clients that use ArchieML's output can then use that order to render the values, allowing you to vary the presentation for each array item. [+books] kicker: Books you should read score: ★★★★★!!! title: Wuthering Heights author: Emily Brontë title: Middlemarch author: George Eliot score: ★★★★☆ [] Each line becomes its own object , with a type and value . ArchieML splits these two words into separate objects to make it easier to deal with different type of information; rendering logic can always be based on the content of the type attribute. Freeforms also allow you to type unstructured lines of text, which are included as items in the array with a type of text . Note that this means that comments do not work within freeforms. [+text] I can type words here... And separate them into different paragraphs without tags. [] Having full control over order is useful when arrays need to be mixed with other types of data . For example, showing a list of events interspersed with general artwork. [+events] header: My Birthday date: August 20th, 1990 {.image} src: https://example.com/photo.png alt: Family Photo {} header: High School Graduation date: June 4th, 2008 [] Multi-line values Values automatically end when a newline is encountered. But all subsequent text is read into a buffer that can be added to that key. Anchor the end of a multi-line value by following the value with a line beginning with ":end". All whitespace within the block is preserved. Try removing the last line to see how it changes the output: key: value More value Even more value :end Works within object and simple arrays [arrays.complex] key: value more value :end [arrays.simple] * value more value :end Escape characters You can place any text inside of a multi-line value. If one of your lines would be interpreted by the parser as a key or some other special command, you may have to escape that line by adding a backslack to the beginning of it. The backslash won't be included in the value. Try removing the backslashes from the following lines: key: value \:end :end key: value \more: value :end key: value [escaping * is not necessary if we're not inside an array, but will still be removed] \* value :end key: value \:ignore \:skip \:endskip :end Block comments Wrap text between lines that begin with ":skip" and ":endskip" to ignore blocks of text. :skip this: text will: be ignored :endskip There is also a safety mechanism of sorts built in. When the parser encounters a line beginning with ":ignore" (even if it's within a :skip block), parsing immediately stops, and the rest of the document is ignored. key: value :ignore [array] * Blah [] other-key: other value Usage If you use JavaScript or Ruby, we hope you'll try one of the existing ArchieML parsers . If you want to make a parser yourself (or want the technical details on the format), the full specification is online here . Questions or concerns? The Github repository for this site is available at newsdev/archieml.org , and you can use its Issues page to submit questions or bugs on the spec itself. Created by Michael Strickland , Archie Tse , Matthew Ericson and Tom Giratikanon / The New York Times Copyright (c) 2015 The New York Times Company

Subscribe another address Creators of Record Two creators went to NYU’s business school, then decided to make a show about the news “Our videos are what we wish we could consume more of.” By Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 14, 2026, 3:43 p.m. The data is in : News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record , an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs. On a September afternoon in Manhattan’s Union Square neighborhood, Shreyas Sinha is sitting on a toilet, wearing a blue suit. Looking into the camera, he asks, “Why is it that everything I’ve been eating this year is giving me diarrhea?” Sinha is about to link the 2026 cyclospora outbreaks to decades of problems at the Food and Drug Administration. “I’m only allowed to make three diarrhea jokes in this video,” Sinha says. “I live in tyranny.” The toilet video is one of the tamer stunts that Sinha and his co-creator, Gaurav Srivatchan , have pulled for their YouTube channel, A Show About The News , a weekly deep dive into major business and politics stories (tagline: “Critics are calling it the worst alternative to mainstream media, and those are just the critics I’m related to.”) In a video about why young people can’t afford to buy homes , Sinha pops out of a cardboard box on the street and takes former New York City mayor Eric Adams to a studio apartment filled with men. Other recent videos include a 45-minute interview on the street with former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, an explainer on prediction market ads , and a rap music video on why retirement investments are safer than get-rich-quick schemes. Sinha, 25, and Srivatchan, 22, met in 2023 when they were students at New York University’s Stern School of Business. They teamed up to make short vertical explainer videos, but those didn’t take off as much as they’d hoped. In 2024, Sinha quit his finance job to pursue A Show About The News full-time, and they transitioned to creating long-form deep dives with a dash of their own humor. In 2025, Sinha and Srivatchan signed a contract to make the show as a franchise of Morning Brew. (They declined to share the specifics of the partnership.) Sinha anchors most videos, with Srivatchan directing, editing, and producing. A Show About The News has 97,000 YouTube subscribers and 84,000 Instagram followers. I chatted with Sinha and Srivatchan about how they launched their media careers, how they use humor to explain the news, and what they think business opportunities are for creators today. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Tameez: Why did you start creating news videos? Sinha: Gaurav and I started making videos together during the spring 2023 semester, when I was a senior at NYU and he was a freshman. I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. It seemed like everything was [pointing to], “Hey, you should start making short-form videos.” And then Gaurav was like, “Hey, I’m actually really good at editing videos.” We were not really thinking of it as a YouTube channel, but as making short-form stories. At the time, we were called Fifty50 Media. We were all about trying to distill the world into bipartisan perspectives. We eventually started focusing more on deeper-dive stories. We renamed ourselves to A Show About the News. It’s very easy to put out a political opinion that goes viral, but we really wanted to focus on good stories. Eventually, we started making videos for Morning Brew, and we joined Morning Brew full-time as a franchise in August 2025. Srivatchan: We realized that building a loyal audience off shorts wasn’t feasible in the long-term. And we constantly [faced] the challenge of bringing in nuance. That’s one of the reasons we started working on long-form videos. We try to bring in the political economy lens from our college education and highlight the underlying principles [of] today’s headlines. Sinha: To be honest, we weren’t successful in short-form. We had made 50 or 60 shorts… Srivatchan: Some of them would pop off, get a million views. But the way people consume on the internet is very different from the way people consume when they go to a theater, [where] they’re paying for an experience and they’re going to watch a specific thing. YouTube and social media are like a theater where you can leave and go watch another movie at any time. That’s the challenge of making videos on the internet. Sinha: After our first video that got a million views, we were like, “Oh shit, this is it.” And it wasn’t. We added followers, but it wasn’t like we were going to get 100,000 people to come back in the next short. We were competing against the new Frozen movie and The Office and Mr. Beast exploding dynamite in his backyard. Tameez: Tell me more about how the Morning Brew deal happened. Srivatchan: I was in London, studying abroad. I slapped a bunch of logos as watermarks on our old videos [and sent them as] demo reels to news outlets. Sinha: We literally got zero responses…then an opportunity came to make a video for [Morning Brew] and it was a great experience. We made another and another, and then they were like, “You guys should just do this for us.” Srivatchan: Morning Brew provided us access to this office. It’s great to not meet under a lofted bed in Shreyas’ apartment. Sinha: They’re an excellent partner [because] they believe in allowing editorial control to be with the person who makes the video. We’re not going into meetings asking, can we do this topic next week? It’s a very high-trust environment, which, from talking to other people who work at other media companies, is extremely rare. Tameez: You guys both left careers in finance to do this full-time. Sinha: It was an economically stupid decision, but I knew that if I failed now, I would be young enough to start again. It’s easy to have the golden handcuffs of waiting until the right time, but there is never a right time. It was taking a bet on myself and someone who I really trusted. Still, our videos were getting 12 views at that time; it wasn’t as if something took off and it was like, “Okay, this can pay our bills.” Srivatchan: I had the advantage of being younger. [Shreyas left] a full-time job. I did my summer internship in consulting and got my return offer, but it was a lot less of a risk for me, personally. It obviously helped that we had some backing from Morning Brew. Tameez: Why is making A Show About the News important now? How does it fit into the larger information ecosystem? Sinha: What we do, in the context of where we went to school, is the equivalent of becoming ballerinas. All of my friends are investment bankers in private equity or in consulting. That is the tried and true method [for NYU Stern graduates]. If you tell people, “Hey, I’m not recruiting for banking, I’m thinking of doing consulting,” they look at you like you just said you want to be an art major. When we said we were going to build a media company, it was truly mind-boggling for people. I loved what Fareed Zakaria did, what Ezra Klein did, but my favorite people when I was a kid were Jon Stewart and John Oliver, Hasan Minhaj and Seth Meyers and Conan O’Brien and Nathan Fielder. I knew I wasn’t going to be a great stand-up comedian, I wasn’t going to be a great writer, but maybe I could combine those to make a job out of it. It’s easy to pat ourselves on the back and say there’s a lot of garbage out there. But also, it has never been a better time to be an independent creator. If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there. Tameez: Tell me about your workflow, from video ideation to posting. Sinha: We don’t do short-form clips [from longer videos]. We script our shorts. That takes a ton of time. [But] long-form is the priority. It takes much more time, but you really get to have a relationship with the audience. Srivatchan: When it comes to shorts, either Shreyas or I will have something that really interests us for the week. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We spend the rest of the time on long-form. We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week. Tameez: What are the things that make a story for A Show About the News? Srivatchan: It has to interest us personally. It really shows, in a video, if we’re doing something just for the views. Our audience is super-interested in tech, AI, and Wall Street stories, so that’s [another] major thing we consider. Sinha: Do we actually have something new to say about it? There’s no point in making a video that someone else has already made. A lot of people have made videos about how people aren’t having kids anymore. That doesn’t mean we wouldn’t [cover that topic], but we need to have something new to say. In our video, we talked about how governments have spent tens of billions of dollars but it hasn’t resulted in any more babies. We talked about demographic trends and got into studies. We brought in a bunch of 19- and 20-year-olds and asked them why they’re not having more sex. Then we went to a bunch of older people and were like, “So, you guys were doing it hella in the 90s. What’s the secret? Let’s give it to these kids.” The combination of all those things is what makes it A Show About the News video. Tameez: Why is it important for you guys to be funny? Srivatchan: It helps us talk about darker topics in a lighter way. Comedy also helps you build more interaction with your audience. It’s the best feeling when [people in the comments] are making jokes. Sinha: We try to be funny, maybe to a deficit. In one of our worst-performing videos , we had a guy come in on an inflatable horse. Gaurav was wearing a Will Smith mask and slapped me. But sometimes it really works. We filmed this thing where we were having a shootout with Abraham Lincoln as he smoked a vape. That did great for us. I listen to a lot of podcasts of serious, smart people. The way they talk, I’m like, how are you not ripping your hair off right now? How are you not just slamming your head against your desk? Our videos are what we wish we could consume more of. Tameez: How do you gather information? Do you do any original reporting? Srivatchan: We have all these sources that we regularly read. For a lot of politics and inside scoops on Capitol Hill, Politico is great. For more niche stories, ProPublica is great. Each source has its own strength. We send stuff to each other all the time. Once we’re in the research phase of a video, we do everything possible to learn about what the scope of the video is and what sources and articles can fall into that. We’d be dishonest if we didn’t mention AI. We don’t use AI at all in our scripting or production process, but Perplexity has been great for finding articles and different things on specific subjects. It’s been a huge timesaver, as well, [since] the internet is dominated by paid articles rising to the top in Google. Tameez: Tell me about the staging and production. Since you guys often film outside, do you have any favorite spots? Have you ever been kicked out of a location? Sinha: The staging is Gaurav and me carrying around our equipment. Srivatchan: We don’t carry around anything too heavy. We use a Sony FX30 on a tripod. Sinha: We’ve only been kicked out of one place ever, which was 1 Worldwide Plaza on 8th Ave. [But] 99% of people are super nice and accommodating and come up and say hi. The reason we’re outside is not only so we can have the hustle and bustle [as the background], but because for the longest time we didn’t have anywhere else to film. Tameez: What is your fact-checking process like? Does Morning Brew lend you any fact-checkers? How do you issue a correction if you need to? Sinha: We do a lot of our own fact-checking. Corrections often occur in the way of Gaurav coming to me and being like, “Shreyas, you moron, you said this and it’s actually this.” Then we record a voiceover, or we change it in the captions, or we just put it up as text. We [request comment from] every company or person we talk about, so if they have something to say, we can try to incorporate it. We do [the fact-checking] ourselves. Tameez: Who is your audience? What is your relationship with them like? Srivatchan: The audience is very much like who we are. They tend to be a ton of college-age or young professionals working in major cities, in finance, consulting, law, or related fields. If they’re in college, they tend to be debate kids or Model UN kids. Tameez: You guys recently started doing weekly livestreams on the street. How’s that going? Sinha: If you go on YouTube right now, high production quality is the expectation. It’s not like when I was young and my favorite YouTubers were clearly filming in their bedrooms. There’s so much money that is being invested into it, which is awesome, but if you want to have authentic relationships with your audiences, you need to do more. [The livestreams] have been so much fun. We talk to people, ask them where they’re from, tell a story, and they have questions. It’s taking our videos to another level. We still have to learn how to grow, bring people to it, and keep them entertained. Srivatchan: Earlier this year, TBPN [Technology Business Programming Network] was sold to OpenAI for $100 million. Their whole thing was live-streaming. They didn’t get that many viewers concurrently on their livestreams — everything was clips, targeting a very specific niche — but we saw how they grew through clips. We also wanted to tackle news topics we don’t have the time to cover in shorts and long-form. Tameez: I’m curious about how you guys sustain yourselves financially. Sinha: When we started making these videos, I was writing articles on the side and freelancing so that I could pay rent. Eventually, this was able to pay rent. By no means are we rich. But we really believe in the business model of digital media. It’s important to incentivize people to invest in media that is fact-checked, that is telling stories that are new and not just polarizing or viral for virality’s sake. You can’t ask people to only think of [media] as a charity expenditure or as a nonprofit, because those are the first things that go away when the market goes down, and the first thing people are going to stop cutting checks to if they don’t see the ROI. We spend most of our time thinking about content, but it’s important to be creative about our business models. We always tell ourselves not to think about ourselves as employees or YouTubers, but to keep reminding ourselves that we’re founders of a startup that is trying to do something for the world. The prevailing narrative that news media is doing poorly is because news media for generations was run by journalists, and that was fine because they could get cable carrier fees. But the reason they were able to do that was because they had a monopoly. You could only watch CNN, CBS, and ABC News because that’s all you had. We blame consumers all the time, saying they should subscribe to newspapers, they should support TV news. We’re losing something really important by these companies being close to bankruptcy. But it’s not the consumers’ fault. There was no innovation from those companies, no leaning into newsletters. Once Morning Brew proved that they could do it, they got into podcasts, and they’re mostly all right. The New York Times is an excellent shop. But I’m yet to see that from ABC and CNN and NBC and MSNBC. There’s been a huge stepping back from actually doing the job of being an inventor of new business models. That’s why we’re in this crisis. We blame consumers, we blame social media, but we really should be blaming media news executives a lot more. There’s a lot of money to be made in this. I want people to know there are people out there trying to build successful business models, not just relying on the charity of investors, rich people, and consumers. Tameez: What is your business model? Sinha: We sell ads, but we also bring in a new audience for Morning Brew that cross-pollinates across other products. When you watch a short-form video on one of Morning Brew’s franchises, you might be more likely to buy ad space in one of their B2B newsletters, or in their podcast, or something else. That’s a really potent business model that allows the content to be not just the product, but also to be part of this larger engine where you can monetize in a bunch of very unique and creative ways. [I asked Sinha and Srivatchan to answer a few final questions via email. Their answers are below.] Tameez: What are your lifestyles like? Do you have families or dependents? Homeowners or renters? Srivatchan: We live in New York City, we rent our apartments. No families or dependents. We have girlfriends who you could say are very, very early investors in us. Tameez: What are some of the unexpected costs of being news creators? Srivatchan: Once you know how the sausage is made, you have the lens on for everything you consume. Being so deep in the process of making news videos means when we watch other creators’ content, we’re constantly analyzing their production process and creative choices. We find ourselves rewinding because we zoned out the actual content. Tameez: How has your relationship to social media and information consumption changed since you started making videos? Srivatchan: One under-discussed crisis with social media is “audience capture.” Basically, a creator is limited to the topics and perspectives that they know do extremely well with their viewers. It’s a tempting force to gravitate into, the constant urge to just give your audience what you know they want and very little else. Tameez: What lessons do you think legacy journalism can learn from news creators and vice versa? Sinha: It’s hard to say what’s legacy and what’s new these days. Morning Brew has never had a TV broadcast or print media arm, but it’s owned by a media conglomerate, Axel Springer. Other news companies, from CNN to The Wall Street Journal, have pretty successful social media presences and journalists who’ve made a name for themselves. The crisis for news companies that dominated in the 20th century is that they relied on fixed distribution: cable, broadband, local stations, and papers. A random Joe couldn’t get their ideas placed in those, so the competition for viewership was highly limited. Today, competition is high. Legacy journalists who struggle often blame the changing tides of information consumption, when in reality they’re just struggling to compete for attention. Many have been successful in making the transition, so we don’t think it’s fair to paint all of legacy journalism as having something to learn from news creators. results.evidenceText: The Book of Shaders Українська - Bahasa Indonesia - Tiếng Việt - 日本語 - 中文版 - 한국어 - Español - Portugues - Français - Italiano - Deutsch - Русский - Polski - English The Book of Shaders by Patricio Gonzalez Vivo and Jen Lowe This is a gentle step-by-step guide through the abstract and complex universe of Fragment Shaders. Contents About this book Getting started What is a shader? “Hello world!” Uniforms Running your shader Algorithmic drawing Shaping functions Colors Shapes Matrices Patterns Generative designs Random Noise Cellular noise Fractional brownian motion Fractals Image processing Textures Image operations Kernel convolutions Filters Others effects Simulation Pingpong Conway Ripples Water color Reaction diffusion 3D graphics Lights Normal-maps Bump-maps Ray marching Environmental-maps (spherical and cube) Reflect and refract Appendix: Other ways to use this book How can I navigate this book offline? How to run the examples on a Raspberry Pi? How to print this book? How can I collaborate? An introduction for those coming from JS by Nicolas Barradeau Examples Gallery Glossary About the Authors Patricio Gonzalez Vivo (1982, Buenos Aires, Argentina) is a New York based artist and developer. He explores interstitial spaces between organic and synthetic, analog and digital, individual and collective. In his work he uses code as an expressive language with the intention of developing a better together. Patricio studied and practiced psychotherapy and expressive art therapy. He holds an MFA in Design & Technology from Parsons The New School, where he now teaches. Currently he works as a Graphic Engineer at Mapzen making openSource mapping tools. WebSite - Twitter - GitHub - Vimeo - Flickr Jen Lowe is an independent data scientist and data communicator at Datatelling where she brings together people + numbers + words. She teaches in SVA's Design for Social Innovation program, cofounded the School for Poetic Computation, taught Math for Artists at NYU ITP, researched at the Spatial Information Design Lab at Columbia University, and contributed ideas at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. She's spoken at SXSW and Eyeo. Her work has been covered by The New York Times and Fast Company. Her research, writing, and speaking explore the promises and implications of data and technology in society. She has a B.S. in Applied Math and a Master's in Information Science. results.pageTitle: The Ultimate Guide to Developing a Successful Business Intelligence Strategy
results.pageDescription: Build a winning business intelligence strategy. This guide covers the key components, steps, and best practices to transform your data into data-driven decisions, improve ROI, and gain a competitive edge in 2026.
results.evidenceText: Business Intelligence Strategy: A 7-Step Guide for Success (2026) Skip to content A business intelligence strategy defines the structure through which data becomes usable: how it’s collected, modeled, governed, and translated into insight that informs action. In large organizations, fragmented pipelines, inconsistent taxonomies, and manual reporting often slow decision cycles and obscure the true performance picture. A well-designed BI strategy eliminates these inefficiencies, ensuring accuracy, scalability, and trust in every metric delivered to the business. This article breaks down how to architect an enterprise-grade BI framework, from data modeling and transformation logic to warehouse integration, metric governance, and visualization alignment. Key Takeaways: Strategy is a Roadmap: A business intelligence strategy is not a single project but a continuous plan that aligns data initiatives with overarching business objectives. Alignment is Everything: The most successful BI strategies are co-created with key business stakeholders to solve specific, high-impact problems. Technology is an Enabler, Not the Goal: The right tools are crucial, but they are only effective when supporting a well-defined strategy and a data-literate culture. Culture Trumps All: Fostering a data-driven culture through training, accessibility, and celebrating wins is essential for long-term user adoption and success. Start with Governance: Establishing clear data governance, quality, and security protocols from the outset prevents future chaos and builds trust in your data. What Is a Business Intelligence (BI) Strategy? A business intelligence strategy is a formal plan that outlines the specific processes, technologies, and cultural frameworks an organization will use to leverage data for improved decision-making. It's the "who, what, when, where, and why" of your entire data analytics ecosystem. This strategic business intelligence approach ensures that every dashboard built, every report generated, and every data point analyzed serves a distinct purpose tied directly to a business outcome. BI Strategy vs. BI Tactic It's crucial to distinguish between strategy and tactics: A BI tactic might be creating a specific sales dashboard or analyzing a single marketing campaign. These are valuable but isolated actions. A BI strategy , in contrast, is the overarching framework that governs these tactics. It defines the rules for data quality, dictates which tools are used, and ensures that the insights from that sales dashboard are shared with the marketing team to inform future campaigns. A strategy provides direction, consistency, and scalability. The Core Components of a Modern BI Strategy A comprehensive BI strategy is built on several key components that work in harmony: Business Objectives: The "why." What specific goals (e.g., increase customer retention by 10%, reduce operational costs by 5%) will BI help achieve? Key Performance Indicators (KPIs): The metrics used to measure progress against objectives. People & Culture: The roles, responsibilities, and training required to create a data-literate organization. This includes executive sponsors, data analysts, and end-users. Data Governance: The policies and procedures for ensuring data is accurate, secure, consistent, and accessible to the right people. Technology & Infrastructure: The tools and platforms for data integration, storage (data warehouses), analysis, and visualization. Implementation Roadmap: A phased plan detailing the timeline, milestones, and resources needed to execute the strategy. The Transformative Impact of an Effective BI Strategy Investing in a well-defined BI strategy is a fundamental business transformation that yields significant returns across the organization. It elevates decision-making from reactive guesswork to proactive, data-informed action. Gaining a Sustainable Competitive Advantage By harnessing BI, companies can identify market trends, anticipate customer needs, and monitor competitor actions with greater speed and accuracy. This intelligence enables you to innovate faster, enter new markets more strategically, and create offerings that truly resonate with your target audience, keeping you several steps ahead of the competition. Enhancing Operational Efficiency and Reducing Costs BI tools illuminate inefficiencies hidden within complex processes. Whether it's optimizing supply chains, streamlining marketing spend, or identifying bottlenecks in the sales funnel, a BI strategy provides the visibility needed to make targeted improvements. This leads directly to reduced waste, lower operational costs, and higher profitability. Fostering Innovation Through Data-Driven Insights Data is the fuel for innovation. A successful BI strategy uncovers previously unseen patterns and correlations, sparking new ideas for products, services, and business models. When employees at all levels have access to reliable data, they are empowered to experiment, test hypotheses, and contribute to the company's growth in meaningful ways. Laying the Groundwork: Pre-Strategy Assessment and Stakeholder Alignment Before you can build a roadmap, you need to know your starting point. A common reason BI initiatives fail is a lack of alignment with the business. This preparatory phase is critical for ensuring your strategy is relevant, supported, and built on a realistic understanding of your organization's capabilities. Identifying Key Business Stakeholders and Champions A BI strategy can’t be developed in an IT silo. It requires active participation from key stakeholders across all major departments, including sales, marketing, finance, and operations. Identify not only the decision-makers but also potential "champions" who are enthusiastic about data and can help drive adoption within their teams. Engaging these stakeholders early and often ensures the strategy addresses real business needs and secures crucial buy-in. Conducting a BI Maturity Assessment Honestly evaluate your organization's current capabilities. Where are you on the BI maturity spectrum? Are you still reliant on manual spreadsheets (nascent), or do you have some departmental dashboards (developing), or are you leveraging predictive analytics (mature)? Understanding your current state helps you set realistic goals and create a phased roadmap that builds capabilities over time. The 7-Step Blueprint for Building Your BI Strategy Roadmap With the groundwork laid, you can now construct the core of your BI strategy. This step-by-step blueprint provides a structured approach to move from concept to a detailed, actionable plan. This is the heart of your business intelligence implementation strategy. Step 1: Define Clear, Measurable Business Objectives and KPIs: Start with the end in mind. Work with your stakeholders to translate high-level business goals into specific, measurable objectives. For example, a goal of "improving marketing effectiveness" becomes an objective like "Increase Marketing Qualified Lead (MQL) to Sales Qualified Lead (SQL) conversion rate by 15% within six months." Then, define the KPIs that will track this, such as conversion rate, cost per SQL, and sales cycle length. Step 2: Assemble a Cross-Functional BI Governance Team: Establish a formal body responsible for overseeing the BI strategy. This team, often called a BI Competency Center (BICC) or data governance council, should include representatives from both business and IT. Their responsibilities include defining data standards, prioritizing BI projects, managing tool selection, and ensuring compliance with security and privacy regulations. Step 3: Select the Right BI and Analytics Technologies: Based on your objectives and user needs, evaluate and select the appropriate technology stack. This includes tools for data extraction and loading (ETL/ELT), data storage, and data analysis and visualization (like Tableau, Power BI, or Looker). Consider factors like ease of use for business users (self-service capabilities), scalability, integration capabilities, and total cost of ownership. Step 4: Develop a Comprehensive Data Management Plan: This plan addresses the entire data lifecycle. It outlines which data sources will be used, how data will be integrated, and the processes for ensuring data quality (cleansing, validation, enrichment). It should also define master data management (MDM) principles to create a "single source of truth" for key entities like customers and products. Step 5: Design a Scalable BI Architecture: This is the technical blueprint for your BI system. It details how data will flow from source systems into a central repository, such as a data warehouse, and then be made available to analytics tools . A well-designed architecture is scalable to handle growing data volumes, flexible to incorporate new data sources, and performant to deliver insights quickly. Step 6: Create an Implementation and Adoption Roadmap: Break the strategy down into manageable phases. A typical approach is to start with a pilot project that addresses a high-impact, low-complexity business problem to demonstrate early value. The roadmap should outline a timeline for subsequent phases, including specific deliverables, resource allocation, and a detailed training and change management plan to drive user adoption. Step 7: Establish a Framework for Measuring ROI: To secure ongoing investment and support, you must prove the value of your BI strategy. Develop a framework to measure its return on investment (ROI). This can include hard metrics like cost savings and revenue increases, as well as soft metrics like time saved on manual reporting, faster decision-making, and improved employee satisfaction. Struggling With Step 5? Let Improvado Handle the Architecture Designing a scalable BI system is complex—but it doesn’t have to be. Improvado unifies data from every marketing, sales, and revenue source, automates modeling and transformation, and delivers clean, governed datasets ready for analysis. Build a flexible, future-proof BI architecture without the engineering burden. Get your demo Choosing Your Technology: BI Tools and Platforms Comparison The BI tool market is vast and varied. Selecting the right platform is a critical decision that directly impacts user adoption and the overall success of your strategy. The primary choice often lies between traditional, IT-led platforms and modern, self-service tools that empower business users. Key Features to Look for in a BI Tool Data Connectivity: The ability to easily connect to a wide range of sources, from databases and cloud applications to spreadsheets. Data Visualization: A rich library of charts, graphs, and maps with interactive drill-down capabilities. Ease of Use: An intuitive, drag-and-drop interface that allows non-technical users to build their own reports and dashboards. Collaboration & Sharing: Features that allow users to share insights, comment on dashboards, and schedule report delivery. Governance & Security: Robust administrative controls for managing user access, data security, and content certification. Scalability: The ability to handle large datasets and a growing number of users without performance degradation. The implementation phase is where the strategic vision meets operational reality. Focusing on these critical pillars ensures a smoother rollout and greater long-term success. Data Governance and Security Protocols Data governance is the foundation of trust in your BI system. Without it, you risk a "garbage in, garbage out" scenario where users don't trust the data and abandon the tools. Establish clear ownership for key data assets, define standard business metrics, and implement robust security protocols to control data access based on user roles and responsibilities. Data Integration and Quality Management Your BI platform is only as powerful as the data it contains. The biggest challenge for many organizations is integrating data from dozens of disparate sources. This is where modern data pipeline platforms become essential, automating the process of combining information from various systems. This process must also include rigorous data quality checks to cleanse, de-duplicate, and standardize data for accurate analysis. Improvado addresses this challenge by providing an end-to-end data infrastructure purpose-built for analytics and BI teams. It automates extraction, transformation, and loading (ETL/ELT) of marketing, sales, and revenue data into your preferred warehouse. Beyond aggregation, Improvado enforces governance rules, maintains schema consistency, and performs quality validation at every stage of the pipeline. With Improvado, you can: Connect to 1,400+ data sources with fully automated data extraction. Normalize and standardize metrics and dimensions across channels for consistent BI reporting. Enforce naming conventions and data governance policies to maintain structural integrity. Apply automated validation, anomaly detection, and error handling for continuous data accuracy. Deliver clean, BI-ready datasets directly into warehouses like BigQuery, Snowflake, or Redshift. Maintain full data lineage and transparency across every transformation step. Access unified datasets instantly through the AI Agent, using natural language queries for ad-hoc insight generation, or use pre-build dashboard templates for Tableau, Looker Studio and Power BI. Build a Reliable Data Foundation for BI at Scale Improvado automates data integration, transformation, and quality assurance across all your marketing, sales, and revenue systems. With governed pipelines and real-time validation, it delivers trusted, warehouse-ready data your BI team can rely on for accurate, enterprise-grade reporting. Get your demo Building Effective and Actionable KPI Dashboards Dashboards are the primary interface between users and data. A poorly designed dashboard can be just as confusing as a raw spreadsheet. The best practice is to design dashboards that tell a story, starting with high-level summaries and allowing users to drill down into details. Effective KPI dashboards are tailored to specific roles and focus on the metrics that matter most for their decision-making process. Improvado review We now rely fully on Improvado for multiple dashboards that we use for day-to-day marketing operations and strategy, as well as for presentations to executive leadership. Waleed Noury Lead Analytics Engineer at Activision Overcoming Common Challenges in BI Strategy Execution Even the best-laid plans encounter obstacles. Being aware of the common challenges in BI implementation allows you to address them proactively rather than being derailed by them. Tackling Data Silos and Poor Data Quality: This is arguably the most common and difficult challenge. It requires both a technical solution (data integration platforms) and an organizational one (fostering cross-departmental collaboration). Managing Change and Ensuring User Adoption: People are naturally resistant to change. A comprehensive change management plan, including communication, training, and support, is not optional – it's essential for success. Balancing Agility with Governance: Business users want speed and flexibility, while IT needs to ensure security and data integrity. A successful strategy finds the right balance, often by creating a "governed self-service" model. Proving Value and Sustaining Executive Sponsorship: Initial enthusiasm can wane if the BI initiative doesn't show tangible results. Continuously track and communicate wins, tying them back to the original business objectives and ROI framework. Best Practices for Long-Term BI Success and Evolution A BI strategy is not a "set it and forget it" document. The business landscape and technology are constantly changing, and your strategy must evolve with them. Adopting these best practices ensures your BI program remains relevant and valuable for the long term. Adopt an Agile and Iterative Approach Avoid massive, multi-year "big bang" projects. Instead, adopt an agile methodology, delivering value in small, iterative cycles. This allows you to gather user feedback early, adapt to changing requirements, and demonstrate progress continuously. Continuously Align BI with Evolving Business Goals Schedule regular reviews (e.g., quarterly) of your BI strategy with key stakeholders. Are the original objectives still relevant? Have new business priorities emerged? This ensures your BI efforts remain focused on what matters most to the organization. Automate Where Possible for Efficiency Manual data preparation and reporting are time-consuming and prone to error. Leverage reporting automation to free up your analysts from mundane tasks so they can focus on higher-value activities like deep-dive analysis and interpreting insights. This significantly increases the efficiency and scalability of your analytics team. Integrate Advanced Analytics and Marketing Attribution As your BI program matures, move beyond descriptive analytics (what happened) to more advanced forms. This includes incorporating diagnostic analytics (why it happened) and predictive analytics (what will happen). For marketers, this means implementing sophisticated models like multi-touch marketing attribution to understand the true impact of every channel. The Future of Business Intelligence: Trends Shaping Enterprise BI Strategy The field of BI is rapidly evolving, driven by advancements in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and cloud computing. A forward-thinking enterprise BI strategy must account for these trends to maintain a competitive edge. The Rise of AI and Machine Learning in BI AI is transforming BI from a reactive tool to a proactive partner. Augmented analytics uses machine learning to automatically surface hidden insights, identify anomalies, and even suggest actions. This makes sophisticated data analysis accessible to a broader audience, reducing the need for specialized data science skills for many common tasks. Predictive and Prescriptive Analytics The future of BI lies in not just understanding the past, but in predicting the future and prescribing the best course of action. Predictive models can forecast sales, identify customers at risk of churn, and optimize inventory levels. Prescriptive analytics takes this a step further by recommending specific actions to achieve desired outcomes. The Growing Importance of Real-Time Analytics In a fast-paced digital world, decisions must be made in minutes, not days. The ability to analyze streaming data from sources like IoT devices, web traffic, and social media analytics in real-time is becoming a critical capability for industries like e-commerce, logistics, and finance. Integrating all of these sources, including your data warehouse, is key to a holistic view. Conclusion A strong business intelligence strategy begins and ends with data. results.pageTitle: Assessing Meta's Plans to Expand Community Notes | Oversight Board
results.pageDescription: This policy advisory opinion examines the potential human rights impacts of expanding the community notes program outside of the United States, recommending specific factors Meta should consider when deciding which countries to omit from the expansion.
results.evidenceText: Assessing Meta's Plans to Expand Community Notes | Oversight Board Skip to content Executive Summary The Oversight Board finds that community notes could enhance users’ freedom of expression and improve online discourse on Meta’s platforms if implemented with sufficient scale, speed and safeguards against manipulations. However, in certain circumstances – including in repressive human rights regimes, in particular electoral contexts and in ongoing crisis and conflict situations – expanding community notes to countries outside the United States could also pose significant human rights risks and contribute to tangible harms that Meta has a responsibility to avoid or remedy. The Board is also concerned about coordinated disinformation networks potentially abusing community notes, and the risk that community notes could, in certain contexts, privilege dominant political, ethnic or linguistic groups, and marginalize minority groups. The likelihood and severity of these potential human rights risks and their adequate mitigation depend greatly on the design and functionality of the community notes product in each context. The effectiveness and adequacy of Meta’s mitigation measures regarding some of these risks – for example, to ensure contributor anonymity and protect against those who try to game the system – will need to be verified through an ongoing process of data gathering and reporting on how community notes function in practice. In addition, insofar as Meta envisions community notes as its primary way to address misinformation falling short of its threshold for removal (i.e., where there is not a likelihood of contributing to the risk of imminent physical harm or to interference with the functioning of political processes), the Board finds that the program’s design may limit its ability to accomplish that goal. Delays in note publication, the limited number of published notes and its dependence on the broader information environment’s reliability raise serious doubts about the extent to which community notes can meaningfully address misinformation linked to harm. The Board recommends criteria that Meta should use to assess when these human rights risks may warrant withholding community notes from a particular market. The Board’s recommendations are necessarily conditional because Meta’s questions cannot be addressed conclusively without sufficient testing and detailed data about how the community notes algorithm functions in real-world situations and in relation to other misinformation tools. For that reason, the Board also recommends ongoing data gathering, assessment and reporting regarding the functionality of community notes, related to those criteria. Background On November 19, 2025, the Board announced that it had accepted a request from Meta for guidance on the specific factors the company should consider when deciding whether any country should be omitted from its planned expansion of community notes outside the U.S., as local context might impact the program’s operations. Additionally, Meta asked the Board how to weigh such factors in relation to one another, in a way that can be applied on a large scale. In its request, Meta said the community notes program is in an “early stage of product development” and the company possesses “limited data from the U.S. beta rollout.” Meta described this rollout as a period of “testing and refinement” that may result in the form of community notes evolving. Because of these considerations, the company’s primary interest lies in establishing “fundamental guiding principles” for its implementation worldwide. Importantly, the Board has not evaluated the general effectiveness of community notes in the U.S. The Board consulted a range of stakeholders, including technical experts on bridging algorithms, civil society organizations, journalists and fact-checkers, for observations and data on different community notes-style moderation systems (including X’s) across different contexts. On January 7, 2025, Meta announced it was introducing a community notes program and ending its third-party fact-checking program in the U.S. The company indicated it would refine community notes before making it available for users outside the U.S. Key Findings and Recommendations Informed by a broad consideration of potential human rights impacts, the Board has developed the following country-level factors to guide Meta’s rollout of community notes: Safeguards in repressive human rights contexts Community notes depends on an active and engaged contributor base. Such programs have experienced greatest success amid a robust civil society. Ideally, contributors rely on independent media to support proposed notes and participate without fear of harassment or retribution. The Board underscores that until Meta can demonstrate robust and effective contributor privacy protections, with evidence of red-teaming under adversarial conditions, a clear policy on handling requests from law enforcement agencies for community notes data and risk mitigation measures, countries with repressive human rights records and weak civil societies should be omitted from the initial rollout. Exercise caution during elections Community notes can support access to information and freedom of expression during elections in robust information environments with free media and uninhibited civil society. Without those conditions, the program risks publishing misleading notes, and Meta should proceed with caution. Where significant risks to the integrity of political institutions are present, and Meta determines through product testing, risk assessment and human rights due diligence that its safeguards are insufficient to mitigate them, community notes should not be introduced in advance of or during major elections. Omit countries with a history of coordinated disinformation networks Community notes operates under the assumption that a sufficiently diverse and independent set of contributors will evaluate content in good faith and that consensus signals can reliably approximate accuracy. Where malicious actors have repeatedly demonstrated the ability to coordinate large numbers of accounts to promote deceptive information, this assumption may not hold. Instead, community notes risks becoming a vector for manipulation rather than a safeguard against it. This risk will become more acute as artificial intelligence facilitates the scaled creation and operation of these networks. Until such time as data on the functionality of community notes can verify the adequacy of Meta’s mitigation measures against such coordinated activity, the Board recommends that Meta initially omit countries with a historical pattern of intentional, large-scale disinformation networks. Meta should also consider here whether actors have demonstrated the intent to manipulate information ecosystems and possess the technical sophistication to do so on a large scale. Do not introduce in crisis or protracted conflict conditions The potential vulnerability of community notes to coordinated manipulation by armed groups, state actors or their supporters seeking to legitimize propaganda through gaming of the note rating system poses heightened risks in ongoing crisis or conflict situations. Conditions causing groups’ inability to contribute, e.g., unstable internet access and insecurity preventing participation, can exacerbate information asymmetries. In such circumstances, timeliness is critical. Delays in note publication suggest community notes may be an inadequate primary safeguard in crises and conflicts, particularly as thresholds for incitement to violence may be lower. Notes targeting specific groups can more easily result in offline harm. Due to uncertainty over community notes’ performance in conflicts and its potential to heighten risk of harm, the Board believes that it should not be introduced in countries experiencing crises or protracted conflict. Delay introducing community notes where there is language complexity that Meta cannot technically and operationally accommodate Community notes requires sufficient representation of a context’s language groups. Where Meta is unable to achieve this, it should delay introducing community notes. Otherwise, language disparities in notes proposed and published could be created or exacerbated, undermining the program as a plural and diverse information source. Additionally, there are potential linguistic and cultural variations in the use and interpretation of community notes, some unexpected, which may affect which notes are published. For example, what it means to rate something as “helpful” might differ in different places and when the word is translated. In countries where Meta anticipates features of community notes cannot yet accommodate linguistic complexity, it should consider delaying its introduction. Exercise extreme caution where social division and disagreement that drives political violence cannot be outlined simply The design of X’s community notes algorithm implicitly assumes disagreement and division in a particular context can be modelled simply, giving a single measurement of polarization. Meta has not provided any information that suggests its program will be different. However, where division and disagreement cannot be easily modelled along a single axis, this can reinforce an unduly simplistic understanding of conflict, overlooking how multiple factors intersect (across politics, ethnicity, religion, language and caste, for example). In practice, this risks marginalizing minority perspectives, as misleading or harmful notes reaching consensus among majority groups may be published. Where the algorithm does not accurately identify and attempt to “bridge” (rewarding content receiving positive feedback from audiences that typically disagree) a division that drives conflict and violence, this risk of harm is especially acute. Therefore, the Board recommends that Meta exercise extreme caution when considering countries characterized by these dynamics. Where there is a heightened risk of misalignment between the design assumptions of community notes about a society and what actually drives social and political division there, such countries need not be categorically omitted from community notes’ rollout. Rather, the rollout should be sequenced to allow performance testing in different contexts, and should begin cautiously in political, linguistic, and information environments that are similar to places where Meta already possesses such data, piloting and risk mitigation measures. Omit countries that face persistent obstacles to internet access The Board recommends omitting countries that face persistent or systemic obstacles to internet access, as community notes relies on broad, consistent and equitable contributor participation to function as intended. A narrow pool of contributors, due to infrastructure gaps, high costs, regional disparities and, especially, government-imposed shutdowns, undermines the core premise of community notes’ representativeness. Weighting The Board recommends that factors whereby community notes could create or heighten the risk of harm should be weighted heavier than factors from the program’s inadequacy as a harm mitigation measure. These include thresholds whereby Meta should not introduce community notes until it demonstrates it can do so while mitigating these harms. Meta should provide the Board with the criteria or risk matrix it develops to guide expansion every six months during initial expansion, with evidence of how these are applied in country-level decisions about program expansion. Data and reporting The potential human rights risks of and adequacy of mitigation strategies for community notes depend on the design and functionality of the product in context. Meta told the Board it plans to test the program prior to launch in a market. The Board recommends this testing should focus on surfacing and mitigating risks related to contributor anonymity, coordinated disinformation campaigns and gaming of the system, language representation, and contributor participation. The Board calls for substantial transparency, reporting and researcher access to data on Meta’s community notes performance. Policy Advisory Opinion in Full 1. Meta's Request On January 7, 2025, Meta announced that it was introducing a community notes program and ending its third-party fact-checking system in the United States. At the time, Meta indicated that it would refine community notes before making it available for users outside the United States. Meta describes community notes as allowing users to add labels with additional context to content where they believe additional information may be helpful. Participants in the community notes program, called “contributors,” rate proposed notes as “helpful” or “not helpful” and explain their response by selecting a reason from a list of options. An algorithm calculates a score that reflects whether a note has been rated helpful among a sufficient number of contributors who usually disagree with each other based on past ratings. If this score reaches a certain threshold, and the note does not violate the Community Standards, then the note will be published. This system contrasts with the third-party fact-checking program, which relies on partner organizations to review, research and make judgments about the veracity of content that can result in labeling false or misleading information. Meta requested guidance from the Board on the specific factors it should consider when deciding whether any country should be omitted from its planned expansion of community notes outside the United States, as local context might impact the program’s operations. Additionally, Meta has asked the Board how to weigh such factors in relation to one another, in a way that can be applied on a large scale. In its request, Meta said that the community notes program is in an “early stage of product development” and that the company possesses “limited data from the U.S. beta rollout.” Meta described this rollout as a period of “testing and refinement” that may result in the form of community notes evolving. Because of these considerations, the company’s primary interest lies in establishing “fundamental guiding principles” for its implementation worldwide. The Board has accordingly not undertaken a general evaluation of the effectiveness of community notes as it has operated in the United States. The Board identified a set of human rights risks that it is most concerned about mitigating in advance of the global rollout of community notes. To do this, the Board consulted a range of stakeholders, including researchers, technical experts, civil society organizations, journalists and fact-checkers, for observations and data on the operation of different community notes-style systems of moderation (including X’s) across different contexts. The Board’s evaluation focuses on the anticipated performance of Meta’s community notes system if applied in other markets beyond the United States in light of that information. Answering the question of what community notes and the algorithm that underpins it will do in a given context depends significantly on empirical data. Meta indicated that the system will be piloted outside of the United States, with performance data evaluated against Meta’s goals for the program. Meta said that it plans to publish downloadable data on community notes, with data categories on par with what X shares for its community notes program. This would include the full text of notes and their associated geographies, ratings for each note, status history, user enrollment and the requests for notes on content. However, that level of data is not yet available for the Board’s use, and instead, a set of high-level metrics was provided confidentially to the Board. Meta provided the Board with certain data on community notes, including but not limited to the number of contributors enrolled, the number of notes written and published, and the average time to consensus in the United States. Therefore, this opinion cannot offer empirical analysis of the successes, failures or impact of Meta’s community notes program. It does, however, incorporate insights from research on similar crowdsourced programs to understand likely areas of risk in different contexts, which directly relate to the questions Meta posed to the Board. Importantly, Meta did not ask the Board to evaluate the effectiveness of its third-party fact-checking program, nor the relative merits of community notes and third-party fact-checking. This opinion therefore, does not include independent recommendations about whether third-party fact-checking should be discontinued or maintained. However, given that community notes is included in Meta’s approach to misinformation, the opinion does consider the absence or presence of third-party fact-checking as a relevant factor in how Meta addresses deceptive content in a given context. The Board asked Meta if this list of countries where Meta has agreements in place to provide third-party fact-checking will remain accurate during and after any rollout of community notes beyond the United States. In response, Meta said that it is “subject to change periodically.” Recent media reporting has found that while Meta has not made a public statement on the future of third-party fact-checking outside of the United States, contracts with fact-checking agencies have been renewed for 2026, albeit at reduced funding levels. The questions posed in Meta’s request indicate that Meta is actively considering extending community notes to countries outside the United States. The Board’s opinion neither endorses nor opposes this approach. Rather, its analysis proceeds by analyzing what the implications would be if Meta were to make community notes available everywhere and addresses what considerations should preclude or condition launching the product in a particular country. The Board accepted Meta’s request on November 19, 2025. Meta’s full request to the Board can be found here . Following this acceptance, the Board sent Meta questions. The Board asked questions on: how Meta envisions the relationship between community notes and other approaches to deceptive information; how the company defines and measures success for community notes; the risk mitigation measures and human rights due diligence Meta undertook in advance of the community notes launch in the U.S., and similar efforts planned for international launches; the performance of community notes in the U.S.; technical differences between Meta’s community notes and X’s community notes; and the relationship of community notes to election-related and crisis- and conflict-related measures. 2. Stakeholder Engagement Over the course of developing this policy advisory opinion, the Board engaged with external stakeholders in the following ways: Public Comments The Board received 23 public comments in December 2025 related to this policy advisory opinion that met the terms for submission . Eight were submitted from United States and Canada; five from Asia Pacific and Oceania; five from Europe; three from Latin America and the Caribbean; and two from the Middle East and North Africa. The issues covered by the submissions included: Potential benefits of community-based moderation to address deceptive content. Several submissions highlighted the positive impacts of community notes on freedom of expression, such as the adding of context and the system’s potential to build information literacy, especially when compared to interventions that result in content being removed (see, for example, PC-315688, Full Fact). These submissions argue that community notes and third-party fact-checking could work as complementary tools.
